# EmptySock Engine — AI Agent Guide

This file is the decision record for the monorepo. It records conventions and non-obvious architectural choices. For API signatures and worked examples, see the docs at `docs/`.

---

## Documentation

The docs follow a Unity/Unreal-style layout — four sections that match different reading modes. Start at `docs/README.md` for a full navigation table.

| Section            | Path                         | What it covers                                                                                    |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Getting Started    | `docs/getting-started/`      | Installation, first game, IDE tour, from GameMaker                                                |
| Guides             | `docs/guides/`               | Task-oriented: physics, input, saving, navmesh, actors, plugins, hot-reload, building             |
| Reference          | `docs/reference/`            | Indexed by class/system — Scene, Entity, all systems. Ctrl+F destination, not sequential reading. |
| Tutorials          | `docs/tutorials/`            | Pong, platformer, visual novel, bullet hell — complete step-by-step projects                      |
| Architecture       | `docs/architecture.md`       | Layers, ECS, Actor Model, IDE data flow (contributor deep-dive)                                   |
| Troubleshooting    | `docs/troubleshooting.md`    | Common pitfalls and how to diagnose them                                                          |
| Glossary           | `docs/glossary.md`           | Canonical term spellings, deprecated aliases, definitions                                         |
| Language Reference | `docs/language-reference.md` | TypeScript & JavaScript reference for engine scripting                                            |

> The legacy `docs/manual/` files remain for backward compatibility with external links. New content goes in the directories above.

---

## Repo layout

Top-level packages: `packages/engine` (@emptysock/engine, the ECS runtime — bitECS-backed, one `Scene`/`Entity`/`Component` model, one export surface), `packages/types` (@emptysock/types, shared interfaces with no implementation), `packages/toolchain` (@emptysock/toolchain + the emptysock-toolchain CLI binary), `packages/network` (@emptysock/network, the optional Colyseus multiplayer companion package — never imported by @emptysock/engine itself), `packages/vn` (@emptysock/vn, VNSystem/Story Graph), `packages/battle` (@emptysock/battle, BattleSystem), `packages/tilemap` (@emptysock/tilemap, TilemapSystem/NavMeshSystem; each an optional module package, a `workspace:*` dependant of @emptysock/engine, never the other way around), and `apps/ide` (Tauri v2 + React/Vite). Each panel in the IDE is a single file under `apps/ide/src/components/panels/`. Editor state lives in one store _tree_ rooted at `apps/ide/src/store/ideStore.ts` (Zustand) plus named sibling stores for specific domains (DB, sequence, localisation, variable, audio, VN, VS, CG state, …) composed alongside it — not literally all inside that one file. Build logic lives in `apps/ide/src/services/`.

`packages/engine/src/` is a flat tree at the package root — `Scene.ts`, `Entity.ts`, `Component.ts`, `Game.ts`, `systems/`, `components/`, `ui/`, `bridge/`, `internal/`. There is exactly one export surface (`src/index.ts`, published as `@emptysock/engine`'s `.` entry); there is no subpath split and no second, parallel object model anywhere in this package.

---

## Non-obvious decisions

### Engine environment boundary

The engine package must not import anything from the DOM, from Tauri APIs, or from `apps/ide`. The reason is that the same compiled engine bundle runs in three contexts: Node.js (Vitest), the browser preview iframe (IDE), and the Tauri WebView (desktop). An import of a DOM-only API causes silent runtime failures in Node, not a compile error. Enforce this by reviewing any new engine import against the allowed list: the TypeScript standard library and other `@emptysock/*` packages only.

### Actor mailbox ordering

`ActorSystem` drains every actor's inbox before calling `update()` on any actor. This means all messages sent during frame N are fully processed before frame N's update() logic runs on any actor. A consequence: messages sent inside an actor's `receive()` are processed in the same flush pass, not deferred to the next frame. If you add a message loop that causes an actor to send back to itself, the flush will run until the inbox is empty — an infinite loop if the actor always re-enqueues.

### Transport and StorageAdapter are interfaces, not classes

`SaveSystem` takes a `StorageAdapter` (`get`/`set`/`delete`/`listKeys`) rather than talking to IndexedDB or a filesystem directly — the engine defines the interface, the host (browser preview shell, Tauri desktop shell) builds and injects the concrete adapter. With no adapter given, `SaveSystem` defaults to `MemoryStorageAdapter` (an in-process `Map`, nothing persisted across restarts), which is what makes it usable out of the box under the headless testing harness and any other Node context. The same "engine defines the interface, whoever has a live instance wires the concrete implementation" pattern shows up again for `QueryChannel` (see below) and would apply to any future networking transport — the engine ships no concrete WebSocket/WebRTC implementation; that belongs in `@emptysock/network` or game code.

### `PluginSystem`, `VariableStore`, `LocalisationSystem`, `ViewportSystem`, and `WindowSystem` are `Game` services, not module-level singletons

Each of these is genuinely process-global — an analytics SDK, a switches/variables store, the one canvas/viewport, or the one OS window all exist once for the lifetime of the app, not per-scene. A bare module-level singleton would make that reachable from anywhere, but it would also be real shared mutable state across every test file in the same process — two unrelated test files touching `variableStore.setSwitch()` would silently interfere with each other via shared Node module caching. Instead, `Game`'s constructor registers real instances of all five with `this.services.register(...)` (`Services.ts`'s `ServiceRegistry` — a typed, explicit replacement for Godot-style autoloads) and hands them to scene code via `SceneLifecycle.plugins`/`.variables`/`.localisation`/`.viewport`/`.window`, the same convenience pattern `SceneLifecycle.audio`/`.input` already use. This keeps the "reachable from anywhere without dependency injection" property (one instance per `Game`, which in practice means one per running process) while making the instance's lifetime and scope explicit and test-isolable — a `new Game()` in one test never shares state with a `new Game()` in another. Game code that needs a shared, process-wide instance should read it from `ctx.plugins`/`ctx.variables`/`ctx.localisation`/`ctx.viewport`/`ctx.window` (inside a scene's `onLoad`/`onUpdate`) or `game.services.get(...)` directly, never construct or expect a bare importable singleton value.

`CameraSystem` deliberately stays out of this list — a camera is naturally per-scene (a scene may want its own camera, or several, or none); game code constructs `new CameraSystem()` and calls `camera.attach(stage)` itself, and neither `Game` nor `RenderPipeline` ever auto-wires one.

### Tauri detection at runtime

Code that needs Tauri capabilities must check `'__TAURI_INTERNALS__' in window` at the call site, not at build time. There is no separate Tauri build and browser build — both modes run the same bundle. Build-time detection (env vars, define flags) would produce two artifacts that need to be maintained separately. The runtime check costs one property lookup per call; the payoff is a single deployable that works in both modes.

### rc-dock owns the full viewport

DockLayout is the sole child of the IDE's root flex container. Never add a sibling element with fixed height alongside it. rc-dock calculates panel sizes from its own bounding box. A sibling that consumes vertical space causes the layout to overflow — the bottom panels become partially hidden and the overflow does not scroll because DockLayout sets its own overflow policy. Add persistent UI (a title bar, a status bar) by making it a DockLayout tab, not a flex sibling.

### No loading screen, no splash screen

The engine does not own a loading screen or a splash screen. The first scene starts immediately once the engine bundle and user bundle have executed — there is no engine-inserted transition, delay, or branded screen before the developer's code runs. Do not add one. If a game needs a loading screen or a splash screen, the developer creates it as a scene like any other (typically the `startScene`), controls its duration with `async onLoad`, and navigates away when ready. The engine's job is to get out of the way.

### GPU flags in lib.rs

`NvOptimusEnablement` and `AmdPowerXpressRequestHighPerformance` are declared as `#[no_mangle] pub static` in the Tauri lib.rs. The `#[no_mangle]` attribute prevents Rust's linker from mangling or eliminating the symbol. The GPU driver on Windows and Linux reads these symbol names from the compiled binary's export table at the OS level — there is no API call involved. If these symbols are removed or marked private, the driver silently falls back to the integrated GPU. This is not detectable at runtime.

### PhysicsSystem3D must be destroyed

Rapier3D allocates its world and body buffers in WASM linear memory, which is outside the JavaScript heap. The garbage collector cannot see this memory. Calling `physics.destroy()` runs Rapier's internal Drop implementation and frees the WASM allocation. If `destroy()` is not called when a scene unloads, the WASM heap grows permanently for the lifetime of the process. On long play sessions that transition between scenes frequently, this causes out-of-memory crashes.

### `onUpdate` must not be async

The game loop calls `onUpdate(dt)` as a plain synchronous function and does not await the return value. If `onUpdate` is declared async, the async/await machinery creates a Promise that is silently discarded. Work scheduled after an await inside `onUpdate` runs at an undefined time, divorced from the game loop's frame budget. The engine also cannot catch errors thrown after an await in `onUpdate`. Use `entity.startCoroutine` for work that spans multiple frames.

### `virtualFiles` must include all open files

The esbuild-wasm virtual filesystem plugin intercepts relative imports at build time by looking up the importer path and the import specifier in the `virtualFiles` map. If a file is open in the IDE but not present in `virtualFiles` when the build runs, the import resolves to nothing — esbuild treats it as an error, but the error message names the specifier, not the missing map entry. Always pass the full `openFiles` record from the IDE store into `GameBuildService.buildNow()`.

### NavMesh data is offline

`NavMeshSystem.load()` accepts a pre-built polygon graph. There is no API to generate the navmesh from a tilemap at runtime. Building a polygon graph from raw tile data requires Delaunay triangulation and polygon merging, which is O(n log n) and would block the main thread for hundreds of milliseconds on a large level. Build the navmesh in the level editor (or a preprocessing step) and ship the polygon data as a JSON asset.

### Component types are identity keys, and a shape change diffs declared defaults

`addComponent`/`getComponent` use the component's registered name string as the key. `ComponentRegistry.ensure()` detects a component _shape_ change — an add/remove/type change to a field — by comparing the `typeof` of every field in a re-registered `ComponentDef`'s _declared_ defaults (`def.createDefaults()`) against a snapshot taken the last time that name was registered — never against the actual values currently sitting in the component's live arrays. This matters because `ensure()` runs on every ordinary access (`entity.get()`, `entity.add()`, `scene.each()`, …), not only after a hot-swap, and a field's runtime value routinely diverges in type from its initial default during normal gameplay — `PhysicsBody.bodyHandle` starts `null` and is later assigned a real numeric handle by `PhysicsSystem`, for one. Diffing against live data would misfire a "shape changed" reset on that kind of ordinary mutation. As a fast path, `ensure()` also skips diffing altogether when the exact same `ComponentDef` object comes back (the overwhelmingly common case — a module-level `const` read every frame): diffing only runs when a _different_ object shows up under the same name, which only happens via a re-evaluated `defineComponent(...)` call, i.e. a hot-swap.

"Affected entities" is scoped per `World` (one per `Scene`), keyed by component name, via the registry's per-world `WeakMap`. A shape change to a component reloads only the entities on the _one world_ that registration call is for, found via a bitECS `query` against that world's still-stable store object before its field arrays are touched — an unrelated `Scene`'s entities (even ones using a component of the same name) are a different `World` and are untouched. The reset itself does not destroy and respawn the entity (which would also wipe its _other_, unrelated components) — it strips and rewrites only the changed component's own field arrays for those entities to the new shape's defaults, in place, on the same store object bitECS already has registered. Entities that never had the component are never queried or touched.

### One `ActorSystem` per scene

Create a new `ActorSystem` in `onLoad` and destroy it in `onDestroy` (`Game.loadScene()`/`loadOverlay()` already do this and hand the instance to scene code as `SceneLifecycle.actors`). A shared `ActorSystem` that persists across scenes would process stale messages from actors that belong to an unloaded scene, since actors from the old scene stay registered and `broadcast()` would invoke them after their scene's `onDestroy` has run — a use-after-destroy bug that's difficult to reproduce.

### Collision/sensor callbacks live in a side-table, not the component's fields

`defineComponent<T extends SerializableRecord>` rejects a shape with a function field at the type level (`Serializable.ts`) — deliberately, so a component made only of `Serializable` fields can be saved/loaded generically later. `PhysicsBody`'s `onCollisionEnter`/`onSensorEnter`/etc. are exactly the kind of field that constraint exists to keep out. `components/PhysicsBody.ts` instead keeps a `WeakMap<World, Map<eid, callbacks>>` side-table and hands out a `Proxy` via `getPhysicsBody(entity)` that reads/writes the real component for ordinary fields and the side-table for the five callback properties — so `getPhysicsBody(entity).onCollisionEnter = fn` still reads as "assigning is the registration" even though the callback and the data never share storage. `PhysicsSystem` dispatches by reading the side-table directly (`getPhysicsCallbacks`), not through the proxy. A future component that wants a callback-shaped property should use the same pattern rather than loosening `SerializableRecord`.

### Scene transitions: `SceneTransitionManager` times them, `RenderPipeline` paints them

`SceneTransitionManager` (`systems/SceneTransition.ts`) takes an `effect: TransitionEffect` but never imports pixi — it stays inside the engine environment boundary (Node/browser/Tauri all run it). It drives a minimal `TransitionEffectSink` interface (`beginTransition`/`transitionProgress`/`endTransition`) via `attachPostProcess()`; `PostProcessSystem` satisfies that shape structurally. Actual pixels come from `RenderPipeline.renderTransitionOverlay(postProcess)`, which reads `PostProcessSystem`'s `transitionEffect`/`transitionProgress`/`transitionColour` and draws a full-screen `Graphics` rect — a triangle wave for `fade`, a growing rect for `wipe`, a rect sweeping across the screen for `slide`. This is an overlay-based transition (one rect on top of whatever's currently rendered), not a true two-scene crossfade — `RenderPipeline` doesn't keep two scenes' sprites live simultaneously.

A true two-scene crossfade is technically buildable (`renderer.render({ target: renderTexture, container })`, pixi v8's real object-form API) but its actual cost (a genuine two-full-render-pass-per-frame hit during the transition window) has no documented number from pixi's own docs and can only really be judged by profiling real target devices, including lower-end tablets — not something a headless CI sandbox can do. Shipping an unvalidated perf-risk rendering path without being able to verify it would be worse than keeping the overlay approach, which is proven and cheap. Revisit only once real device profiling is actually possible.

`SceneTransitionManager` is not a singleton — game code constructs its own `new SceneTransitionManager()`. It also owns no scene registration or pause/resume stack: `Game.ts` already owns scene swapping (`loadScene()`/`loadOverlay()`/`unloadScene()`) with its own lifecycle guarantees, so `SceneTransitionManager`'s only job is timing a transition's visual progress and calling a caller-supplied `load` callback once the duration elapses.

### export-utils has no desktop packaging path — use packages/toolchain/src/desktopBuild.ts

`packages/toolchain/src/desktopBuild.ts` is the one real desktop export path: it scaffolds an actual Tauri v2 project and runs `cargo tauri build`. If desktop export logic needs to change, change it there. `exportWeb`/`exportAndroid`/`exportIOS`/`exportRaspi` live in `packages/export-utils` since `desktopBuild.ts` doesn't cover those targets, but nothing currently calls them from the CLI either.

### GMS2 `.yyp`/`.yy` are not strict JSON, and other real-format quirks

Learned by testing the importer once, end to end, against a real full GameMaker export provided temporarily by the user solely for that purpose; the project data was deleted from disk immediately after and was never committed. Permanently captured as synthetic regression tests in `packages/toolchain/src/__tests__/gms2-import.test.ts`. The quirks:

- `.yyp`/`.yy` files are **not strict JSON** — GameMaker's IDE always writes a trailing comma before the final `}`/`]` of every object and array. Strip `,(\s*[}\]])` → `$1` before parsing.
- The project's own display name lives at `.yyp` root under `"%Name"`, not `"name"`.
- Object events go well beyond `Create_/Step_/Draw_/Destroy_`: collision handlers are `Collision_<other object name>.gml`, keyboard handlers are `KeyPress_<vk code>.gml`/`KeyRelease_<vk code>.gml` (37-40 = arrow keys). Emit `onCollideWith<Other>()`/`onKeyPress<Name>()`/`onKeyRelease<Name>()`.
- Room `.yy` layers identify their kind via `resourceType` (`"GMRInstanceLayer"`, `"GMRTileLayer"`, `"GMRBackgroundLayer"`, …), never `"layerType"`.
- Sprites store one PNG per frame at the sprite directory root, named by that frame's own UUID (`.yy` `frames[].name`), never `<sprite name>.png`.
- `defaultScriptType: 1` does **not** reliably mean "uses GML Visual" — do not warn on it alone.
- Real projects carry legacy GameMaker 8.1 DnD-compatibility symbols (`action_move`, `gml_pragma`, etc.) in compiled action lists. `gml_pragma` and anything else with no engine-side equivalent still surface untranspiled (unresolved identifiers) rather than being faked — but the DnD action library itself now has a real compat layer; see "GMS2 DnD action-library compat" below, which replaces what used to be a blanket "leave these untranspiled" rule for the whole action library.
- A `GMRBackgroundLayer` with a real `spriteId` (a tiled/parallax background image, as opposed to a plain solid-colour compatibility layer with `spriteId: null`) is common in real rooms and is fully converted: `convertGms2Room` captures it as `RoomLayer.backgroundSprite`, and `convertGms2RoomBackgrounds` (`gms2-room-import.ts`) turns each one into a real `Transform`+`Sprite` `SceneFileEntity` on `@emptysock/engine`'s built-in `"background"` render layer (`LayerSystem` already defines one, drawn behind `"default"`/`"foreground"`/`"ui"`), sized to cover the room and merged into the room's generated `.scene.json` alongside its `prefabInstances`. This is a direct `SceneFile.entities` entry rather than a `prefabInstances` entry, because a GMS2 background image has no corresponding GameMaker object and therefore no `.prefab.json` to reference. A background sprite that genuinely fails to convert (missing from disk, no frames) is reported by name in the migration report and left out of the generated scene, rather than silently dropped.
- A resource type this importer has no import path for at all (extensions, timelines, and anything else not audited against a real project) must still produce a named warning, not just a silent entry in the returned `skipped` array — `migration-report.md` is the one place a developer actually reads after running the import, and an asset invisible there is effectively undocumented data loss. Sounds, fonts, and notes are no longer in this bucket — see below.
- **Sounds** convert fully: `convertGms2Sound` (`gms2-sound-import.ts`) reads the sound's `.yy` (via the shared `parseGmsJson`) for `volume`/`loop`/`audioGroupId`, locates the real audio file alongside it (`soundFile` field if present and it actually exists on disk, else the first recognised audio extension found in the directory — not every GMS2 version writes `soundFile` the same way), and `buildSoundAsset` copies that file into `assets/sounds/` and emits a `assets/<name>.sound.ts` descriptor shaped for `@emptysock/engine`'s real `AudioSystem.load(id, src, options)`/`.play(id)` API — there is no separate "AssetManifest" concept in this engine to target.
- **Fonts** convert to metadata only, deliberately: `convertGms2Font` (`gms2-font-import.ts`) reads a font's real `.yy` field `fontName` (the typeface family — not `name`, which is just the resource's own name, e.g. `font0`) plus `size`/`bold`/`italic`. `@emptysock/engine`'s text rendering (`ui/UISystem.ts`'s `Label`/`ButtonState`/`Checkbox`) is plain Canvas/CSS font strings, not a bitmap-font/glyph-atlas renderer, so a GMS2 font's pre-rendered glyph atlas PNG has no real target to convert into and is never copied — `buildFontAsset` emits family/size/style metadata (plus a precomposed `cssFont` string, since `Label` has no separate bold/italic fields) and the import emits a warning explaining the atlas was intentionally not used, rather than silently dropping it.
- **Notes** (`resourceType: "GMNote"`, including GameMaker's own auto-generated compatibility-report notes) are IDE-only documentation with no equivalent concept in `@emptysock/engine`, and this importer does not fabricate one. `convertGms2Note` (`gms2-note-import.ts`) reads the note's real `.txt` content and `buildNoteMarkdown` copies it verbatim into `notes/<name>.md`. The migration report tracks this with its own `"copied"` status, distinct from `"converted"` — the content is preserved and readable, but it never becomes a real engine-native asset the way a sprite/sound/font/room does, and the report says so honestly rather than overclaiming.
- **Tilesets and tile layers convert for real, including a room that uses several distinct tilesets.** A real `GMTileset` `.yy` has a `spriteId: { name, path }` reference to a real `Sprite` resource (confirmed against a real fixture — see `NPC-Studio/yy-typings`'s `data/tileset/test.yy`), but GameMaker's own IDE _also_ bakes a ready-to-use tile-sheet atlas directly into the tileset resource's own directory, alongside its `.yy`: `output_tileset.png`. This is confirmed against a real, full GameMaker project export — every real `GMTileset` resource directory in it had this file, laid out on a grid fully derivable from, and byte-verified against, the `.yy`'s own fields: `(tileWidth + 2*out_tilehborder) * out_columns` pixels wide, `(tileHeight + 2*out_tilevborder) * ceil(tile_count / out_columns)` pixels tall (e.g. `tileWidth: 8`, `out_tilehborder: 2`, `out_columns: 8` produces exactly a 96px-wide PNG — `(8+2*2)*8`). `convertGms2Tileset` (`gms2-tileset-import.ts`) **prefers this baked atlas** when it exists: no second resource to chase, and `columns`/`rows`/`margin`/`spacing` all come straight from `.yy` fields rather than being inferred from an unrelated image's pixel dimensions. `out_columns` is this atlas's real column count (`rows = ceil(tile_count / out_columns)`); `out_tilehborder`/`out_tilevborder` is a per-tile padding/bleed border baked around _every_ cell (not a single sheet-wide margin) — working through `@emptysock/tilemap`'s own tile-sampling formula (`RenderPipeline.mountTilemap()`: `sx = margin + col * (tileWidth + spacing)`) against this layout shows `margin = out_tilehborder` and `spacing = 2 * out_tilehborder` reproduce the real per-cell pixel offsets exactly. `out_columns` was previously documented here as unusable — "GameMaker's own internal runtime texture-page packing width, not the source sheet's natural column count" — which is true of the _referenced sprite's own packing_, but not of this baked atlas: for `output_tileset.png` specifically, `out_columns` is exactly its real column count, confirmed byte-for-byte.

  The `spriteId` chase is now the **fallback path**, used only when `output_tileset.png` is genuinely missing from the tileset's own directory (an older GameMaker workflow, a manually-assembled project, or a resource never re-baked after editing) — `convertGms2Tileset` then follows `spriteId` via the existing `convertGms2Sprite` and derives columns/rows from that sprite's real pixel dimensions (`floor((imageSize - offset + sep) / (tileSize + sep))`), exactly as this importer originally did unconditionally. A tileset with neither a baked atlas nor a resolvable `spriteId` fails with a clear, honest error naming both attempted paths. `buildTilesetAsset` emits `assets/<name>.tileset.ts` — a real `TilesetConfig` for `@emptysock/tilemap`'s `TilemapSystem`, image copied alongside it — from whichever path resolved. `TilesetConfig` has only one `spacing`/`margin` value each (no separate x/y), so an asymmetric baked border (`out_tilehborder` ≠ `out_tilevborder`) or an asymmetric fallback-path separation/offset (`tilehsep`/`tilevsep` or `tilexoff`/`tileyoff`) each get a real, honest warning naming the dropped axis rather than silently averaging or guessing.

  A room's previously-parsed-but-discarded `RoomLayer.tiles` data (`convertGms2Room`'s `parseTiles()`) becomes a real `TilemapData` module (`buildRoomTilemapModule`, `gms2-tileset-import.ts`) — a dense grid, one cell per room-tile-grid position (`{ tileIndex: -1 }` for empty, matching `TileCell`'s own sentinel), sized from the room's own width/height divided by the tileset's tile size — for every distinct, successfully-converted tileset that room's tile layers reference. `@emptysock/tilemap`'s real `TilemapData` shape carries exactly one `tileset` field (unchanged — this was deliberately not extended to a per-layer tileset, since one `TilemapData` module per tileset needed no type change at all), so a room with N distinct tilesets gets N sibling `TilemapData` modules rather than one incomplete one: `rooms/<name>.tilemap.ts` for a room that uses exactly one tileset (unchanged naming, for backward compatibility), or `rooms/<name>.<tileset>.tilemap.ts` per tileset for a room that uses several — a real, common case (e.g. a ground tileset plus a separate props/decoration tileset on their own layers), not a hypothetical edge case; confirmed against a real GameMaker project whose rooms genuinely reference two distinct tilesets each. A tileset that itself failed to convert still gets a real, per-tileset warning naming exactly which tiles were affected, rather than silently dropping that portion of the room's tile data or refusing to convert the room's other, successfully-converted tilesets. A generated `<room>[.tileset].tilemap.ts` imports its tileset module directly (`import { XTileset } from "../assets/<tileset>.tileset.js"`) so the two files can't drift apart on tile size/column count; loading several sibling modules into the same room is one `TilemapSystem.register()`/`.loadInto(scene, name)` call per module — wiring that (or into a room's own `SceneDefinition.onLoad`) is left to the game (or a future `GmsProjectRuntime` follow-up), the same "toolchain emits data, game code wires it up" split every other GMS2-imported asset in this importer already follows.

  **A real GameMaker room `.yy`'s tile layer format is not what it looks like from the schema alone — confirmed against a real, full GameMaker project's exported rooms, not assumed.** Two quirks, both load-bearing (getting either wrong meant every real room's tile data silently parsed as empty, with no error, before this was caught by testing against real project data rather than only synthetic fixtures):
  - A `GMRTileLayer`'s `tilesetId` reference lives directly on the **layer object itself**, as a sibling of `tiles` — never nested inside `tiles.tilesetId`. (`gms2-room-import.ts`'s `parseTiles()` checks the real, top-level field first and only falls back to the nested shape for this module's own pre-existing synthetic test fixtures, which predate this discovery and use the nested shape.)
  - Placed-tile data is `tiles.TileSerialiseData` — a **flat**, row-major array of `SerialiseWidth * SerialiseHeight` raw cell values — never the nested 2D `TileData` array this importer originally assumed (no real GameMaker export has been observed to use `TileData` at all). Each raw cell value bit-packs the real tile index into its low 29 bits and GameMaker's rotate/mirror/flip placement flags into the top 3 bits (`raw & 0x1fffffff` recovers the real index); a cell whose _masked_ index is `0` is empty — this was verified empirically against real, fully-populated ground layers, whose overwhelming majority of cells shared one exact raw value (`0x80000000` — the flip flag alone, masked index `0`) that only ever appeared where no tile was visually placed, while every genuinely-placed tile in that same real data carried a small raw value with no flag bits set. `TileCell` (`@emptysock/tilemap`'s real shape) has no rotate/mirror/flip field, so those bits are read (to correctly recover the real tile index) but not preserved anywhere — the same "honestly read, then honestly not representable" shape `asymmetryWarning` above already uses for a different field. A cross-referenced end-to-end check against real project data — every one of a real room's 12,288 tile-grid cells, independently re-decoded from the room's raw `TileSerialiseData` bytes and compared against this importer's generated `TilemapData` output — found zero mismatches.

- **A stale/orphaned object reference** — an object name still listed in the `.yyp`'s `resources` array whose `objects/<name>/<name>.yy` no longer exists on disk (common in long-lived real projects, where a resource gets deleted from disk without being fully removed from the project file) — is reported as a real, named `"manual"` failure ("object's .yy not found on disk, likely a stale/orphaned project reference"), not silently treated as a successful conversion with a fabricated empty prefab. `importGMS2Project`'s object loop checks `fs.access` on the object's `.yy` before calling `buildObjectPrefabJSON`/`buildObjectBehavior` at all — no `.prefab.json`/`.behavior.ts` is written for it, and it's left out of `convertedObjects` (so it's neither referenced by a room's `prefabInstances` nor listed in `project-manifest.json`). This mirrors the exact check `convertGms2Sound`/`convertGms2Font`/`convertGms2Note` already perform for their own resource kinds. An object whose directory _does_ exist but genuinely has zero `.gml` event files (no custom code, just properties) is a real, valid, different case and still converts normally — only a missing `.yy` is a failure.

### GMS2 room camera/view import — real, and actually wired to a live CameraSystem/RenderSystem, not just parsed

Before this pass, `gms2-room-import.ts` had zero references to "view"/"camera" at all — a room's real GameMaker camera/view data (up to 8 `views[]` slots plus a room-wide `viewSettings.enableViews` switch) was untracked entirely, despite `compat/gmlCamera.ts` (`camera_create_view`, `view_set_camera`, `buildActiveGmlCameraViewports`) and `RenderSystem.renderMultiCamera()` already existing and already tested. This closes that gap end to end: parsed from the real `.yy`, carried through the generated `.scene.json`, and actually applied to a live camera/render pass when a room loads — not JSON nobody reads.

**The real `.yy` schema**, confirmed against the GameMaker manual's `view_xport`/`view_yport`/`view_wport`/`view_hport` reference pages, the `NPC-Studio/yy-typings` GMS2 `.yy`/`.yyp` typings project, and ENIGMA's `room_set_view` compatibility docs (which spells out the identical field list GameMaker's own runtime function takes — `vis, xview, yview, wview, hview, xport, yport, wport, hport, hborder, vborder, hspeed, vspeed, obj` — confirming field names and order independently of the typings source): a room's `.yy` has a top-level `views` array (up to 8 entries, index = view slot) of `{ visible, xview, yview, wview, hview, xport, yport, wport, hport, hborder, vborder, hspeed, vspeed, objectId }`, plus a `viewSettings: { enableViews, ... }` object (`inheritViewSettings` for "use the parent room's settings" is not chased by this importer — a room relying on inheritance with no explicit `enableViews` of its own is treated as `false`, an honest default rather than a fabricated inherited value). `xview`/`yview`/`wview`/`hview` are the world-space rectangle the camera looks at; `xport`/`yport`/`wport`/`hport` are the screen-space rectangle it draws into; `hborder`/`vborder` are the follow-margin in pixels; `hspeed`/`vspeed` are the follow catch-up speed in pixels/step (`-1` is GameMaker's own "snap instantly" sentinel, the same convention this compat layer's other speed fields already use); `objectId` is the object _type_ this view follows — GameMaker resolves this to "the first active instance of that object type" every step, not a fixed instance id.

`gms2-room-import.ts`'s `RoomView` (parsed by `convertGms2Room`'s new `parseViews()`) is the toolchain-internal shape using GameMaker's own short field names; `buildRoomSceneFileViews()` renames these onto `@emptysock/engine`'s runtime-facing `SceneFileView` (`SceneFile.ts`) — `worldX`/`worldY`/`worldWidth`/`worldHeight`, `screenX`/`screenY`/`screenWidth`/`screenHeight`, `borderX`/`borderY`, `speedX`/`speedY`, `followObject` (the object-type name, or absent) — the same "GameMaker's ugly short names live only in the parsing layer, never in generated/runtime data" rule this file's "None of the real `.yy`/`.yyp` format quirks... live in the codegen layer" line already establishes for every other GMS2 field. `gms2-import.ts` merges `views`/`viewsEnabled` straight onto the generated `.scene.json` alongside `prefabInstances`/`entities`, the same merge-after-`buildRoomSceneJSON()` shape `convertGms2RoomBackgrounds`'s entities already use. A room with active (`visible: true`) views gets a real note in `migration-report.md` naming the count and whether it'll go through `CameraSystem` or `RenderSystem.renderMultiCamera()`, rather than the view data landing silently.

**Actually wired, in `GmsRuntime.ts` — the "makes it work end to end" integration point.** `buildSceneDefinition()`'s `onLoad` calls `compat/gmlCamera.ts`'s new `configureGmlViewsFromRoom(ctx, file.views, file.viewsEnabled)` right after `loadSceneFile()`, before any GML `onCreate` runs — one `camera_create_view`-equivalent handle per view slot (view slot 0 mirrors onto this file's pre-existing default camera id 0, which is what actually drives a live `CameraSystem` when `options.camera` was given; every other active slot gets its own real, independently-tracked handle with no live rendering behind it on its own — see `GmlCameraContext`'s pre-existing doc comment for why only id 0 was ever mirrored to a live camera), bound via `view_set_camera`, with `view_set_visible`/`view_set_*port` mirroring the room's real screen rectangle. This means a Create-event GML call reading `camera_get_view_x`/`view_camera[idx]` on frame 1 already sees the room's real view state, not defaults.

**Camera follow is real, not just stored-and-ignored.** `GmlCameraHandle` previously stored a `targetObject` field with an explicit doc comment stating it drove no actual motion — a genuine, previously-honest gap. `configureGmlViewsFromRoom` now also stamps a new `followObjectName` field (the object-type name, resolved the same way `resolveGmlObjectType`/`onCollideWith<Type>` dispatch already resolve object types — via `Meta.name` — duplicated locally in `gmlCamera.ts` rather than imported, to avoid a `systems/GmlCollision.ts` import cycle neither file otherwise needs), and `stepGmlCameraFollow(ctx, camid)` applies GameMaker's real border-follow algorithm every step (confirmed against ENIGMA's `room_set_view` docs and community references for the `hborder`/`vborder`/`hspeed`/`vspeed` semantics, since the manual documents the fields but not the exact formula): the view only moves once the followed instance crosses within `borderX`/`borderY` pixels of the view's own edge, moving just far enough to keep it that many pixels inside — never re-centring — and `speedX`/`speedY` caps how far the view itself may move in one step toward that position (`-1` snaps instantly), producing GameMaker's characteristic catch-up scroll rather than a hard teleport. `GmsProjectRuntime.runGmlPasses()` calls `stepAllGmlCameraFollows(ctx)` (steps every configured camera handle, not just the default) once per frame, before the Step passes — matching GameMaker's own per-step ordering, where the camera follows and then gameplay logic runs against the already-moved view. A followed object type with no live instance is a real, honest no-op (GameMaker's own behaviour: the view simply stops moving), not an error.

**Multi-camera compositing is real too, when a room actually has more than one active view.** `GmsProjectRuntime.update()` calls `game.update(dt)` as before (which renders the single default camera via whatever `SceneRenderer` was attached, exactly as every other room already worked), then — only when `buildActiveGmlCameraViewports()` reports more than one visible, camera-bound view slot — runs a second real pass: `RenderPipeline.renderMultiCamera()` (already-real, already-tested, previously-unused-by-any-caller passthrough to `RenderSystem.renderMultiCamera()` — see this file's own "Multi-camera rendering" entry above) composites every active viewport onto the canvas, overwriting the single-camera frame `game.update()` just drew. This is a genuine second full frame's GPU cost on a multi-view room — the same honest N-render-pass-per-frame caveat this file's `renderMultiCamera()`/`syncLighting()` entries already raise for their own N-pass techniques, not free, not profiled here, and never paid at all by a room with 0 or 1 active views (the overwhelmingly common case, and the only case any real GMS2 project tested against this importer so far has used).

Tests: `packages/toolchain/src/__tests__/gms2-room-views.test.ts` (real `.yy` view-array parsing including the trailing-comma quirk, `viewsEnabled` default-`false` honesty, `buildRoomSceneFileViews`'s field-rename correctness including an absent `followObject`); `packages/engine/src/__tests__/gmlCamera.test.ts` (`configureGmlViewsFromRoom` wiring every slot's camera binding/visibility/screen-rect, `stepGmlCameraFollow`'s border/speed/snap math against hand-derived expected positions, a no-live-instance no-op, `stepAllGmlCameraFollows` covering more than one camera); `packages/engine/src/__tests__/GmsRuntime.test.ts` (a room's real `SceneFile.views` data live on the camera registry immediately after `loadRoom()`, before any `update()`; `update()` actually moving the camera toward a follow target across frames; a room with no views data never throws across repeated `update()`s).

### GMS2 import emits prefab/scene JSON plus a companion behavior module — never a class

`buildObjectPrefabJSON(name, projectRoot)` emits a real `.prefab.json` (`PrefabFile` shape — every GameMaker object instance has a position, so every generated prefab gets a `Transform` component) and now actually reads the object's real `<name>.yy` (via the shared `parseGmsJson`) to layer on real structural data, not just `Transform`: a real `spriteId` (not `null`) adds a `Sprite` component wired to `./assets/sprites/<sprite name>/frame_0.png` (the same convention `buildSpriteAsset`/`convertGms2RoomBackgrounds` use), and `physicsObject: true` adds a `PhysicsBody` component with `type` (`"kinematic"` from `physicsKinematic`, else `"dynamic"` — GameMaker's physics has no static/kinematic distinction this importer can reliably read, so a GameMaker-static object still comes through as `"dynamic"`, a real documented gap), `isSensor` (from `physicsSensor`), and `density`/`friction`/`restitution` (from their `physics*` equivalents) — only fields `PhysicsBody`'s real shape (`packages/engine/src/components/PhysicsBody.ts`) actually has are ever emitted. `PhysicsBody.shape` is deliberately never overridden — GameMaker's `physicsShape` enum has no verified mapping onto `PhysicsBody`'s `"box"|"circle"|"capsule"` without a real project's `.yy` to check the enum values against, so the component's own `"box"` default is left in place. An object with neither a real `spriteId` nor `physicsObject: true` still gets exactly the previous `Transform`-only prefab. `buildRoomSceneJSON()` emits a real `.scene.json` (`SceneFile` shape, one `prefabInstances` entry per room instance whose object was actually imported — i.e. present in `convertedObjects`, not merely listed in the `.yyp`'s resource array, so a stale reference is never emitted as a broken prefab instance either).

GML event code (Create/Step/Draw/Destroy/Collision/KeyPress handlers) is genuine executable behavior, and a `PrefabFile`'s components must stay plain `Serializable` data — the same constraint that keeps `PhysicsBody`'s collision callbacks in a side-table rather than the component's own fields. Transpiled GML logic structurally cannot live inside a `.prefab.json`. `buildObjectBehavior()` transpiles each GML event via the transpile pipeline and emits plain exported functions (`onCreate(entity)`, `onUpdate(entity, dt)`, `onCollideWithX(entity, other)`, …) into a companion `<name>.behavior.ts` module that imports `Entity` from `@emptysock/engine`. Wiring these functions up to real prefab instances (a per-prefab-name dispatch table, most likely) is left to the game importing the project — the engine has no single opinionated "GMS2 object behavior" runtime to hand this off to automatically. `projectManifestJSON()` emits a plain JSON file listing every prefab/behavior/scene file produced — there's no "register a component" step for JSON loaded via `parsePrefabFile`/`loadSceneFile` directly.

None of the real `.yy`/`.yyp` format quirks documented above (trailing commas, `%Name`, event naming, `resourceType` room layers, sprite frame UUIDs, `defaultScriptType` non-signal, untranspiled GM8.1 DnD symbols) live in the codegen layer — they live entirely in the parsing layer (`gms2-parse.ts`/`gms2-sprite-import.ts`/`gms2-room-import.ts`/`gms2-transpile.ts`).

### GMS2 DnD action-library compat

GameMaker 8.1's drag-and-drop action library (`action_move`, `action_create_object`, `action_if_collision`, etc.) used to be documented here as a deliberate gap — "leave these untranspiled rather than faking them" — on the theory that DnD action semantics were too context-dependent to model generically. That was too pessimistic: GM8.1's action library has fixed, well-documented, mechanical semantics (a compass-direction bitmask, relative-vs-absolute coordinate flags, sprite/room/instance references), and it now has a real implementation.

`packages/engine/src/compat/gmlActions.ts` is a sibling to `compat/gml.ts`, not an extension of it — `gml.ts` covers pure/global GML _scripting functions_ (`ds_map_*`, `string_*`, …), none of which touch a specific entity, while every DnD action is imperative and entity-affecting (move this instance, kill this instance, go to this room). Every exported action function takes `(entity: Entity, ctx: GmlActionContext, ...gmlArgs)` — `GmlActionContext` (`{ scene, game?, rooms?, roomOrder?, currentRoom?, prefabs?, sounds? }`) is the same "engine hands out an explicit context, game code supplies the project-specific parts" dependency-injection shape `SceneLifecycle`'s `ctx.plugins`/`ctx.variables` already establish — a generated behavior module cannot know a GameMaker room's engine-side `SceneDefinition` or an object's registered `PrefabDef` on its own, so the game wires `rooms`/`prefabs`/`sounds` in; only `scene` is required.

What's implemented, and how:

- **`action_move`** sets a per-entity velocity from a 9-bit compass bitmask (see `MOVE_DIRECTION_BITS`'s doc comment for the exact bit-order/angle convention used, kept consistent with `gml.ts`'s existing `lengthdir_x`/`lengthdir_y` angle convention) and a speed; applied every step by `gmlActionsStep` rather than integrated immediately, matching GameMaker's own "set it once, the runtime keeps applying it" semantics. `action_move_to`/`action_snap`/`action_set_friction`/`action_set_relative` cover the rest of the movement family — `action_move_to` repositions immediately (a one-shot jump, not a sustained motion) and supports GameMaker's per-action "Relative" flag.
- **`action_sprite_set`/`action_sprite_color`** write straight into the entity's `Sprite` component (`texturePath`/`tint`/`alpha`), converting GameMaker's `0xBBGGRR` colour order into `Sprite.tint`'s `0xRRGGBB`.
- **`action_kill_object`** is `scene.destroy(entity)`. **`action_create_object`/`instance_create`** spawn `ctx.prefabs[objectName]` via `scene.spawn()` — `undefined` plus a console warning (never a thrown error) when the object name isn't wired, the same "honest error over a fabricated result" shape `QueryChannel` uses.
- **`action_next_room`/`action_another_room`** call `ctx.game.loadScene()` against `ctx.rooms`/`ctx.roomOrder`/`ctx.currentRoom` — all optional, because a project that never uses a room-changing action shouldn't have to build this map; a warning names exactly what's missing when they're needed but absent.
- **`action_set_alarm`** ticks down in a per-`(World, eid)` side-table (`ensureMotion`'s `alarms` map — one shared side-table with movement state, not a second scheduling primitive layered on top of `Coroutines.ts`; an alarm is fundamentally "decrement an int every step," which doesn't need coroutine machinery) and fires an `onAlarm(index)` callback once, at zero — one-shot, matching GameMaker.
- **`action_sound`** calls `ctx.game.audio.play(id)`, resolving `soundName` through an optional `ctx.sounds` map. This genuinely depends on the separate GMS2 sound-import work landing a real `{ GameMaker name -> playable asset id }` shape; until then, `soundName` is passed straight through as the id, which is a clean no-op via `AudioSystem`'s own "unknown id" handling rather than a fake resolution scheme invented ahead of that work.
- **`action_if_collision`/`action_if_aligned`/`action_if_empty`** are real conditional checks (AABB overlap against a fixed default half-extent — no texture-size lookup is available from engine-side compat code; `PhysicsBody` is the real answer once a project needs pixel-accurate collision — grid alignment, and "is any other entity within bounds of this point," respectively) whose _nesting_ is a codegen concern: `gms2-transpile.ts` wraps the following generated statement(s) in a real `if (...) { ... }` block (see below) rather than emitting a flat, non-conditional sequence.
- **`action_if_mouse`/`action_if_question`** are implemented (`(button, isDown) => isDown(button)` and `(message, ask) => ask()`) but are the one deliberately-unautomated case: their real signature needs a live predicate callback the transpiler cannot synthesize from a bare GML source argument by text substitution. `action_if_question` in particular has a real, unavoidable semantic mismatch — GameMaker's own "Question" action is a blocking modal dialog, and `onUpdate` must not be async (see above), so there's no engine-owned "block until UI answers" primitive to fake this against. `gms2-transpile.ts` leaves both call sites untranspiled (the same "surface as an unresolved identifier, don't fake it" rule genuinely unmodelled GML like `gml_pragma` already follows) — a developer wires these to `GmlActions.action_if_mouse`/`action_if_question` by hand with a real callback.

Codegen (`gms2-codegen.ts`): every generated event handler (`onCreate`/`onUpdate`/`onDraw`/`onDestroy`/`onCollideWithX`/`onKeyPress*`/`onKeyRelease*`) now takes a trailing `_ctx: GmlActionContext` parameter, and the generated `.behavior.ts` module imports `* as GmlActions from '@emptysock/engine'` alongside `Entity`/`GmlActionContext` — this is what gives every threaded action call in the transpiled body something to act against. `gms2-transpile.ts`'s `THREADED_ACTIONS` pass rewrites a plain-data action call (e.g. `action_move(32, 4)`) to `GmlActions.action_move(_entity, _ctx, 32, 4)`; a separate line-based nesting pass then wraps an `action_if_collision`/`action_if_aligned`/`action_if_empty` line's following non-empty line in a real `if (...) { ... }` block — GameMaker's own compiled DnD action lists are one statement per line, and an "if" action's real semantic is "the next action only runs if this one's condition holds," so this pass reads the transpiler's own line-oriented output the same way.

`gmlActionsStep(entity, onAlarm?)` applies stored `action_move` velocity/friction and ticks `action_set_alarm` timers for one entity; it's meant to be called once per entity per Step. There is no automatic per-frame dispatcher that calls a GMS2-imported prefab's generated `onCreate`/`onUpdate`/`onDraw` functions at all yet — per the "GMS2 import emits prefab/scene JSON..." entry above, wiring those functions to live prefab instances is still left to the game importing the project. `gmlActionsStep`'s own `onAlarm` callback parameter, specifically, is wired for real by `GmsProjectRuntime` — see that entry below for `GmlBehaviorSystem.dispatchAlarm()`, the real per-alarm dispatch it calls into.

### GameMaker's "hypothetical position" collision-query family (`place_meeting`/`place_free`/`collision_*`)

GameMaker's classic solid-wall collision technique — call `place_meeting(x, y, obj)` at a _hypothetical_ next position before actually moving there, and back off if it would overlap something — is THE mechanism a huge fraction of real GameMaker platformers/top-down games use, and it's a real, implemented compat family now: `compat/gmlCollisionQueries.ts`, a sibling to `gmlActions.ts` rather than an extension of it (every function here is still entity-affecting — the calling instance's own mask matters — so it keeps the same `(entity, ctx, ...gmlArgs)` signature `gmlActions.ts` established, but this is a pure-query family with nothing to nest or dispatch, a different shape from `GmlCollision.ts`'s event-dispatch focus).

None of these move the calling instance — the "hypothetical" half of the semantic is real: `place_meeting(entity, ctx, x, y, obj)` reads `entity`'s current sprite-derived half-extents but never writes its `Transform`, checking the AABB overlap as if `entity` were already at `(x, y)`. `place_snapped(entity, ctx, hsnap, vsnap)` is the one exception with no scene query at all — GameMaker's own real signature has no `x`/`y`, it always checks the instance's _current_ position.

What's implemented:

- **`place_meeting`/`place_free`/`place_snapped`** — whole-mask checks against `entity`'s own hypothetical extents. `place_meeting` matches a named object type (or `all`/`noone`); `place_free` matches any `Meta.solid`-flagged instance instead (see below), independent of object type.
- **`position_meeting`/`position_free`/`instance_place`/`instance_position`** — the single-_point_ variants (no `entity` mask involved at all) plus the "return the actual instance, not just a bool" variants, matching GameMaker's own naming split. `instance_place`/`instance_position` return `Entity | undefined` — `undefined` standing in for GameMaker's `noone`, since there's no numeric "no instance" sentinel in this engine's `Entity` API.
- **`collision_rectangle`/`collision_circle`/`collision_line`/`collision_point`** — the general arbitrary-shape-vs-object-type family, each taking `prec` (always a no-op — no per-pixel mask data exists anywhere in this engine, honestly falling back to bbox checking, the same precedent `action_if_collision` already established) and `notme` (excludes the calling instance when `true`, GameMaker's own default).

**Object-type resolution** reuses `systems/GmlCollision.ts`'s `resolveGmlObjectType` (keyed off `Meta.name`) so this file and `onCollideWith<Type>` dispatch can never disagree about what an object-name argument resolves to. `all` matches every instance; `noone` matches nothing — GameMaker's own two special object-reference constants, checked by string equality before falling back to name resolution.

**This is not GameMaker's Box2D-based physics engine, and never should be treated as one.** Every function in this family is a synchronous bbox-vs-bbox geometry check against `Transform`/`spriteHalfExtents`, run once when called — there is no simulated world, no mass/velocity/restitution, no continuous integration, and nothing here talks to Rapier. GameMaker's real physics is a _separate, opt-in_ system (`physics_world_create`, `physics_fixture_create`/`_add_*_shape`, `physics_apply_force`/`_impulse`, `physics_joint_*`, a body's `phy_*` instance variables) that a GML project must explicitly turn on per-room — `place_meeting`/`place_free`/`collision_*` work identically whether or not a project ever calls `physics_world_create` at all, exactly like they do in real, non-physics GameMaker games. Confirmed: this codebase has **zero** compat wiring for the `physics_*`/`phy_*` family anywhere — not in `compat/`, not in `gms2-transpile.ts`. This is a real, deliberate, honest gap rather than an oversight: `PhysicsBody`/`PhysicsSystem` (Rapier-backed, see "PhysicsSystem3D must be destroyed" above) is this engine's actual real-physics answer, and a GMS2 project that never calls a `physics_*` function has nothing to import — building a full Box2D-semantics compat layer speculatively, with no real project exercising it, would be exactly the kind of unvalidated, unmodelled surface this file's other honest-gap entries (`action_if_question`, `image_index`/`image_speed`) already warn against. If a real project that actually uses GML's opt-in physics ever needs importing, that's the moment to design a `physics_*` → `PhysicsBody`/`PhysicsSystem` mapping — not before.

**`Meta.solid`** — GameMaker objects carry a real per-object "Solid" checkbox (`.yy`'s `solid` field), independent of whether the object also has a `PhysicsBody` — a classic non-physics GML game's solid walls are just solid-flagged instances, not physics bodies. `Meta` (already the one component `onCollideWith<Type>` dispatch and the Inspector both read for per-instance identity) gained a `solid: boolean` field for `place_free`/`position_free` to check against. `gms2-codegen.ts`'s `buildObjectPrefabJSON` reads the object's real `.yy` `solid` field and emits a `Meta` component override (`{ solid: true }`) when it's `true` — additive, the same "only emit when it actually differs from the default" shape the existing `physicsObject`/`spriteId` overrides already use.

**Transpiler wiring**: unlike GM8.1's DnD actions (always their own statement, always followed by `;`), this family is real GML _expression_ syntax — just as commonly called inside `if (...)`, a `&&` chain, or an assignment's right-hand side, with no trailing `;` of its own. `gms2-transpile.ts`'s `THREADED_ACTIONS` rewrite pass used to unconditionally append a semicolon after every rewritten call (safe for DnD's always-a-statement shape); that would have corrupted `if (place_meeting(...))` into `if (GmlActions.place_meeting(...);)`. The pass now captures the trailing `;` (if any) instead of assuming one, and echoes back exactly what was there — fixing this family without changing DnD's existing always-`;` behaviour at all. These functions are threaded the same `THREADED_ACTIONS` list DnD actions use, not a second rewrite pass — `if place_meeting(x + 4, y, obj_wall) { ... }` (already unwrapped to `if (place_meeting(...)) { ... }` by an earlier bare-condition pass) becomes `if (GmlActions.place_meeting(_entity, _ctx, x + 4, y, obj_wall)) { ... }`.

### GML behavior dispatch: three Step passes, a Collision pass, a separate Draw GUI pass

The GMS2 DnD action-library compat entry above covers what a transpiled action call _does_; this entry covers what actually _calls_ a GMS2-imported prefab instance's generated `onCreate`/`onStepBegin`/`onUpdate`/`onStepEnd`/`onCollideWith<Other>`/`onDraw`/`onDrawGui`/`onDestroy` functions in the first place — previously nothing did (and `onCollideWith<Other>` in particular stayed dead code even after the Step/Draw passes landed, since most GMS2-imported objects are plain `Transform`+`Sprite` with no `PhysicsBody` for `PhysicsSystem`'s own, unrelated `onCollisionEnter` side-table callback to ever fire against), per the "GMS2 import emits prefab/scene JSON..." entry's own "wiring these functions up to real prefab instances ... is left to the game" caveat.

`components/GmlBehavior.ts`'s `GmlBehaviorState` (`{ behaviorId: string }`) and `registerGmlBehavior`/`getGmlBehavior` registry are `VisualScriptState`'s exact shape, reused rather than reinvented: a generated `.behavior.ts` module's exports are real, static, imported code (not authorable at runtime the way a `VisualScriptGraph` is), so the game registers the module once under an id and many entities can reference the same id.

**Why `GmlBehaviorSystem.update()` is three full Step passes, not one interleaved pass.** GameMaker's real per-frame semantics (confirmed against GameMaker's own manual's Event Order page and community documentation of its event order) is: every instance's Begin Step event completes before any instance's Step event begins; every instance's Step completes before any instance's End Step begins. A single pass calling `onStepBegin`/`onUpdate`/`onStepEnd` back-to-back per entity would let entity B's Begin Step observe entity A's _this-frame_ Step write — GameMaker's own engine never allows that, because it finishes an entire event category across every instance before starting the next category. `update(scene, dt, ctx)` is therefore three separate `scene.each()` sweeps over every `GmlBehaviorState` entity, each one fully completed before the next starts: this is the only way to give the "no instance's Begin Step ever observes a Step write from the same frame" guarantee GameMaker's own instances rely on. `GmlBehaviorSystem.test.ts`'s cross-entity ordering test is a real behavioral proof of this, not just "no exception thrown" — it fails under a naive interleaved implementation.

**A real 4th pass, after Step and before Draw: Collision.** `update()`'s `resolveCollisions()` runs once, after the three Step passes, matching GameMaker's own event order (Step family completes, then Collision, then Draw). GameMaker's real default (non-physics) instance collision model is plain bounding-box overlap checked every step, firing each instance's Collision event specific to the _other_ instance's object type — an object can declare separate `Collision_A`/`Collision_B` handlers, independently triggered only by overlap with that specific type, never every Collision handler the entity has. `systems/GmlCollision.ts` holds the shared matching logic (`resolveGmlObjectType`/`checkGmlAabbOverlap`/`dispatchGmlCollision`) so it has exactly one implementation, not two that could drift: "object type" is resolved via `Meta.name` (the engine's one existing "editor/tooling-visible name" component — see the `QueryChannel`/`Meta.name`/`Meta.tags` entry below), which `SceneFile.ts`'s `loadSceneFile()` now stamps onto a spawned prefab instance from its `PrefabDef.prefabName` whenever nothing already set one, specifically so a GMS2-imported room's prefab instances resolve back to their GameMaker object name here; AABB extents reuse `compat/gmlActions.ts`'s existing `spriteHalfExtents` fallback (`action_if_collision`'s own bbox source), so the two "is GML-A touching GML-B" checks in this engine can never disagree. `resolveCollisions()` is broad-phase-then-narrow-phase: every `GmlBehaviorState` entity is a potential collision _source_ (only a source needs a compiled module to dispatch through), every `Transform`-bearing entity is a potential _target_ (a target needs no `GmlBehaviorState` of its own — GameMaker's own Collision event can be triggered by any instance), and `checkGmlAabbOverlap` is the actual narrow-phase test per pair.

A `physicsObject: true` GMS2 object still has a real Collision event in GameMaker even though it also gets a `PhysicsBody`, so `PhysicsSystem` optionally dispatches the same GML handler on a genuine Rapier contact: `attachGmlDispatch(ctx)` opts a `PhysicsSystem` instance into calling `dispatchGmlCollision` (both directions) from `_drainCollisionEvents` on collision-start, reusing the exact same `GmlCollision.ts` matching helper rather than a second, physics-flavoured copy of it. Unset (the default), a physics contact never touches GML dispatch at all — `PhysicsSystem` otherwise has no GML concept and must not require one to function, the same "engine defines the interface, whoever has a live instance wires the concrete implementation" pattern `StorageAdapter` already uses.

**Why Draw GUI's camera-independence is a render-tree structural property, not a per-call check.** `RenderSystem` gained a `guiStage` container that is a _sibling_ of `stage` (the container `CameraSystem.attach()` transforms), never a descendant of it — both are children of a new, internal-only `_root` container that's the actual thing passed to `renderer.render()`. `CameraSystem` only ever writes `stage.x`/`.y`/`.scale`/`.rotation`; a sibling container is structurally unreachable by that write no matter what the camera does. This is why `RenderPipeline._renderGmlDraw()` needs no camera-transform-reset logic at all — GameMaker's real "Draw GUI draws in screen space, Draw draws in world space" semantic falls out entirely from _where in the tree_ each draw target's `Graphics` is parented (`onDraw`'s into the `"foreground"` layer container, a descendant of `stage`; `onDrawGui`'s into `guiStage`), not from any runtime check in the dispatch code. `_renderGmlDraw()` is a genuine third pass in `renderFrame()` (after sprite sync and particle sync), not a conditional bolted into `_syncOne()`'s per-sprite loop — a per-sprite special case could not express "draw into a structurally different container tree" at all, since that method only ever writes into one sprite's already-assigned container.

**What `draw_*` actually draws into now.** `compat/gml.ts`'s `draw_set_colour`/`draw_rectangle`/`draw_circle`/`draw_text`/`draw_line` used to take a `CanvasRenderingContext2D` — a real, if unused, crack in the engine-environment-boundary rule (a DOM type reference, even if never actually wired to a live canvas). They now take a plain structural `GmlDrawTarget` interface instead. `RenderPipeline`'s new `PixiGmlDrawTarget` is the one real implementation: a pixi `Graphics` (vector shapes) plus `Text` children (pixi's `Graphics` has no text primitive of its own) for `draw_text`, rebuilt from scratch on every `onDraw`/`onDrawGui` call — the same "simplicity over per-frame allocation cost" tradeoff CLAUDE.md's own "ParticleEmitter renders through a real pixi ParticleContainer" entry already accepts. `GmlActionContext` gained an optional `drawTarget` field that `GmlBehaviorSystem.renderDraw()`/`renderDrawGui()` set only for the duration of one dispatch call each, so a `draw_*` call made from `onUpdate`/`onCreate` (outside a draw dispatch) sees `undefined` and no-ops honestly rather than drawing to a stale target.

**The real limits of this pass, stated honestly.** `Scene.spawn()`/`Scene.destroy()` do not call `onCreate`/`onDestroy` automatically — core `Scene`/`Entity` must not grow a required dependency on this optional compat layer, the same boundary `@emptysock/network`'s entity-mapping entry draws for its own optional add-on. `onCreate` dispatch's real integration point is `loadSceneFile()`'s new `onSpawned` option (called once per spawned entity, immediately after every component is attached and every prop applied) — a GMS2-imported room's `.scene.json` loaded through `loadSceneFile()` is exactly where a game wires `GmlBehaviorSystem.dispatchCreate()` in. `onDestroy` dispatch's real integration point is `GmlBehaviorSystem.destroy(scene, entity, ctx)` — the sanctioned way to destroy a `GmlBehaviorState` entity when its `onDestroy` handler matters, since `Scene.destroy()` itself has no `GmlActionContext` (no `Scene`/`Game`/`prefabs`/`rooms` map lives on the core `Scene` type) to dispatch one with. `action_kill_object` (GM8.1's "Destroy Instance") still calls `ctx.scene.destroy(entity)` directly and does not yet route through this — a real, separate follow-up for whoever wires GML behaviors into `action_kill_object`'s call sites next, not silently glossed over here.

`gms2-codegen.ts`'s event-file mapping now reads the real per-suffix `.gml` files GameMaker actually writes: `Step_1.gml`/`Step_0.gml`/`Step_2.gml` → `onStepBegin`/`onUpdate`/`onStepEnd` (GameMaker's own `ev_step_begin`/`ev_step_normal`/`ev_step_end` eventnum values — 1/0/2 — confirmed against GameMaker's manual's Event Order page), and `Draw_0.gml`/`Draw_64.gml` → `onDraw`/`onDrawGui` (`64` is GameMaker's long-standing `ev_draw_gui` eventnum constant). `onStepBegin`/`onStepEnd`/`onDrawGui` are emitted only when the corresponding `.gml` file actually exists — unlike `onCreate`/`onUpdate`/`onDraw`/`onDestroy`, which always emit a stub, these three are genuinely optional (`GmlBehaviorModule`'s fields are all optional, and `GmlBehaviorSystem` treats a missing export as "no handler for this pass", not an error), so emitting an empty stub for every object that never used Begin/End Step or Draw GUI would bloat every generated file for no reason. Draw Begin/End and Draw GUI Begin/End sub-variants are a real, separate, not-yet-covered gap.

### `GmsProjectRuntime`: the one place that actually drives a GMS2-imported project

Everything the two entries above document — `GmlBehaviorSystem`'s Step/Collision/Draw passes, `TimelineSystem`, `GmlSequenceSystem`, `gmlActionsStep`, `PhysicsSystem.attachGmlDispatch` — is real and callable, but until `packages/engine/src/GmsRuntime.ts` landed, nothing called all of them together, in the right order, against a live `Game`. `GmsProjectRuntime` is that orchestration: `new GmsProjectRuntime(game, data, options)` (constructed by the caller — a `GmsProjectRuntime` never constructs its own `Game`, the same "engine owns what it creates, but a `Game` is the caller's to construct" split every other engine entry point uses), `await runtime.loadRoom("room0")`, then `runtime.update(dt)` once per frame.

`GmsProjectData` (the constructor's second argument) is already-parsed, in-memory data — a room-name-keyed `Record<string, SceneFile>`, a `roomOrder` array, an object-name-keyed `Record<string, PrefabDef>`, a `ComponentLookup`, and an optional sound-id map — never a directory path or a file read. This mirrors `loadSceneFile`/`parsePrefabFile`'s own "engine takes already-loaded JSON, never reads files itself" shape (the engine-environment-boundary rule: no fs/DOM import in `packages/engine`). Building a `GmsProjectData` from a real GMS2-import output directory (reading every `.prefab.json`/`.scene.json`, parsing them, and — the genuinely host-specific part — importing/registering every generated `.behavior.ts` module via `registerGmlBehavior`) is left to the caller; a Node build imports `.behavior.ts` modules directly, a browser bundle needs them pre-bundled, and this class has no opinion on which.

`loadRoom(name)` builds one `SceneDefinition` per room (`buildSceneDefinition()`) whose `onLoad` calls `loadSceneFile()` with a real `onSpawned` hook — the exact integration point the "GML behavior dispatch" entry's "real limits of this pass" paragraph names — dispatching `GmlBehaviorSystem.dispatchCreate()` on every spawned entity that carries `GmlBehaviorState`, and whose `onUpdate` runs this class's own per-frame GML passes (`GmlBehaviorSystem.update()`, then `gmlActionsStep()` for every `GmlBehaviorState` entity, then `TimelineSystem.update()`, then `GmlSequenceSystem.update()`) before returning control to `Game.update()`'s own actor/physics/coroutine/render order. `runtime.update(dt)` itself is a thin forward to `game.update(dt)` — every GML-specific pass runs from the `onUpdate` hook `loadRoom()` already installed, not from a second, parallel update loop this class drives independently. This keeps `Game`'s own "the engine owns everything it creates" per-frame order as the one source of truth; `GmsProjectRuntime` adds a hook into it rather than reimplementing or racing it.

**Alarm dispatch is real, not just alarm-countdown.** `gms2-codegen.ts` names a generated alarm handler `onAlarm0`..`onAlarm11` per `Alarm_<n>.gml` source file (GameMaker has 12 alarm slots) — a real, confirmed shape (`gmlActionsStep`'s own doc comment says `gms2-codegen.ts` appends these specifically for its `onAlarm` callback parameter to call). Until this was wired, nothing ever passed that callback: `runGmlPasses()`'s `gmlActionsStep(entity)` call had no second argument, so `action_set_alarm`'s countdown still ticked but `onAlarm?.(index)` always resolved `undefined` and every real GameMaker Alarm event silently no-opped — a significant, previously-undiscovered gap, since Alarms are an extremely common GameMaker pattern (delayed actions, periodic behavior, state-machine timers). `runGmlPasses()` now passes a real closure — `(index) => this._behaviors.dispatchAlarm(entity, index, ctx)` — and `GmlBehaviorSystem.dispatchAlarm(entity, index, ctx)` is the real dispatch: it resolves the entity's compiled module via `GmlBehaviorState.behaviorId` (the same resolution every other `GmlBehaviorSystem` dispatch method already does) and looks up `onAlarm<index>` via `getGmlBehaviorHandler` — the same dynamic-lookup-by-name mechanism `onCollideWith<Other>` dispatch already uses, reused rather than reinvented, since a per-index handler name is generated per-project and can't be a fixed `GmlBehaviorModule` field. Routed through the same `safeCall` every other `GmlBehaviorSystem` dispatch method uses, so one entity's throwing `onAlarm` handler can't abort dispatch for any other entity, or any other alarm firing the same frame. A missing `GmlBehaviorState`, an unresolvable module, or an alarm index with no matching handler on the module are all safe no-ops — most real objects only ever arm a couple of the 12 possible slots.

**Key dispatch is real too, and — unlike Alarm — needed genuine up/down-transition tracking, not just a missing callback wire.** `gms2-codegen.ts`'s `buildKeyFns()` names a generated handler `onKeyPress<Name>`/`onKeyRelease<Name>` per `KeyPress_<vk>.gml`/`KeyRelease_<vk>.gml` source file (`vkNames`/`vkMethodName` map the common vk codes — 8/13/16/17/27/32/37-40 — to labels like `Space`/`Left`, anything else falls back to `Vk<code>`), and nothing ever called either one — confirmed by grep, zero references anywhere in `GmsRuntime.ts`/`GmlBehaviorSystem.ts` before this pass, the same class of previously-undiscovered gap the Alarm fix above found for a different event family. GameMaker's real semantic ("fires once on the frame a key transitions, not every frame it's held") has no existing engine-side primitive to hang onto the way Alarm's own internal countdown does — `InputManager` exposes `isDown`/`keyboard.isDown(code)` (a frozen-per-frame snapshot, see "Input snapshot: frozen by copy, not by timing" above) but no `justPressed`/`justReleased` of its own, so `GmsProjectRuntime` tracks the up/down transition itself: a single `Map<vkCode, boolean>` instance field (`_prevKeyDown`), polled once per frame in a new `dispatchKeyTransitions()` step that runs before `GmlBehaviorSystem.update()`'s Step passes. This is a plain instance field, not a `(World, eid)`-keyed side-table, because keyboard state is genuinely global — one physical keyboard, not per-entity state the way `PhysicsBody`'s callbacks or `VisualScriptState`'s evaluation scope are.

`compat/gmlKeys.ts` is the new home for two small, hand-kept-in-sync mirrors of `gms2-codegen.ts`'s own naming: `VK_NAMES`/`vkMethodName` (the exact same table, duplicated because `@emptysock/engine` cannot depend on `@emptysock/toolchain` — an offline-codegen CLI package, not a runtime dependency, the same boundary that keeps every other engine/tool pairing in this codebase one-directional) and `vkToDomCode` (a new translation this pass needed regardless: GameMaker's `vk_*` constants reuse the legacy numeric `KeyboardEvent.keyCode` numbering, but `InputSystem` tracks keys by the real DOM `KeyboardEvent.code` string, so a vk code has to be translated before it can be checked against `input.keyboard.isDown(...)` at all — a vk code with no known translation is honestly skipped, never guessed). `GmlBehaviorSystem.dispatchKeyPress`/`dispatchKeyRelease(entity, vkCode, ctx)` mirror `dispatchAlarm`'s exact shape: resolve the module via `GmlBehaviorState.behaviorId`, look up `vkMethodName(prefix, vkCode)` via `getGmlBehaviorHandler`, call through `safeCall`. `dispatchKeyTransitions()` computes the frame's pressed/released vk codes once (not once per entity — the transition itself is a single global fact) and offers them to every `GmlBehaviorState` entity, relying on the same "no handler for this name is a safe no-op" behavior `dispatchAlarm` already established for a missing alarm index, rather than inspecting which handlers each module actually exports first.

**Room transitions triggered from inside GML stay in sync with `runtime.currentRoom`.** `compat/gmlActions.ts`'s `action_next_room`/`action_another_room` call `ctx.game.loadScene(ctx.rooms[name])` directly — they have no reference to the `GmsProjectRuntime` instance that built `ctx`, by design (they're free functions callable with any `GmlActionContext`, not just one this class built). To keep `runtime.currentRoom` accurate even when a room change is driven this way rather than through `runtime.loadRoom()`/`runtime.nextRoom()`, `buildContext()` populates `ctx.rooms` with the exact same `SceneDefinition`s `buildSceneDefinition()` builds for `loadRoom()` — each one's own `onLoad` closure updates `this._currentRoom` — so a transpiled `action_next_room` call spawns entities, dispatches `onCreate`, and installs the per-frame GML passes exactly as if `runtime.loadRoom()` had been called, and `currentRoom`/`scene` stay correct afterward either way.

`options.camera`/`options.renderer` are optional live systems this class merges into one `GmsRuntimeContext` (`GmlActionContext & GmlCameraContext & GmlParticleContext` — the three compat files' context types are already structural supersets of the same base shape, confirmed by reading all three, so one merged object satisfies all three with no adapter needed: `gmlCamera.ts` and `gmlParticles.ts` both already spell their extra field `camera`/`particles` consistently with what `CameraSystem`/`RenderPipeline` actually are). When `options.renderer` is given, `loadRoom()` calls `RenderPipeline.attachGmlBehaviors(behaviors, ctx)` after each load, which is what makes `onDraw`/`onDrawGui` dispatch actually happen — that wiring already existed on `RenderPipeline` itself (`attachGmlBehaviors()`/`_renderGmlDraw()`), this class just calls it. With no renderer given, the runtime is fully headless: `update()` forwards to `game.update(dt)`, whose own render step (`Game`'s documented "no renderer attached" no-op) never runs, matching the rest of the engine's headless-testing story.

`destroyEntity(entity)` is the sanctioned way to destroy a `GmlBehaviorState`-carrying entity through this class — it calls `GmlBehaviorSystem.destroy(scene, entity, ctx)` (dispatches `onDestroy`, then the real `scene.destroy(entity)`), never a bare `scene.destroy(entity)`, for the same reason `GmlBehaviorSystem.destroy()`'s own doc comment gives: `Scene.destroy()` has no `GmlActionContext` to dispatch an `onDestroy` handler with.

**Honest gaps, not glossed over.** GameMaker objects do not declare a timeline/sequence on the object resource itself — confirmed against real `.yy` object files while researching this pass, a timeline is only ever assigned imperatively from GML (`timeline_index = tlFoo;`). `buildObjectPrefabJSON()` (`gms2-codegen.ts`) was deliberately _not_ changed to emit a fabricated static `TimelineState` link on a prefab — there is no such link in a real GameMaker project to codegen from, and inventing one would misrepresent GameMaker's actual semantics. `gms2-transpile.ts` now rewrites a bare `timeline_index = tlFoo;` assignment for real (manual.gamemaker.io's `timeline_index`/`timeline_running` reference pages, confirmed live for that pass): it quotes a bare asset-name identifier into the exact string `registerGmlTimeline()` already registers it under, and emits either `entity.add(TimelineState, { timelineId: "tlFoo", position: 0, running: true })` or a field write via `.get()` when the component is already present (re-targeting, since `Entity.add()` has one-shot semantics) — exactly the operation this paragraph used to describe as not-yet-wired. `timeline_index = -1` (GameMaker's own documented "no timeline" sentinel) rewrites to `entity.remove(TimelineState)`. `timeline_running`/`timeline_speed`/`timeline_loop`/`timeline_position` are rewritten on both the write and read side, straight onto `TimelineState`'s matching fields; a bare read of `timeline_index` itself is deliberately left unrewritten (`TimelineState.timelineId` is a string, GameMaker's real `timeline_index` is a numeric asset index with `-1` as its sentinel, and there's no lossless way to answer `timeline_index != -1` from a string id without inventing a fake numeric encoding). Proven end to end by `gms2-timeline-codegen.test.ts` (a real object's Create event produces this exact text) and `GmsRuntime.test.ts` (the exact emitted call shape, executed for real via `GmsProjectRuntime`, attaches/re-targets/removes a live `TimelineState`).

`sequence_index = sqFoo;` was researched for this same pass and turned out not to exist — GameMaker has no per-instance `sequence_index` instance variable; real Sequences are asset/layer-scoped (`layer_sequence_create(layer, x, y, sequence)`, confirmed against manual.gamemaker.io's Sequences reference pages), never a per-instance assignment the way `timeline_index` works.
