If it were released, bitECS's own "next `addEntity()` gets the freed id" recycling could hand that id to a completely unrelated `spawn()` elsewhere before this prefab's pool claims it back, which would break "this pool only reuses slots this prefab previously owned." The consequence: `entity.isAlive` on a pooled-and-destroyed entity's old handle reads `true`, not `false` — unlike a normal (non-pooled) `destroy()`, where the handle goes properly stale. Game code holding that old handle sees the practical equivalent of "destroyed" anyway (`.get()` returns `undefined` for every component, since none are attached), but do not write code that branches on `isAlive` to detect "was this entity destroyed" for a pooled entity — check `.has()`/`.get()` against the components you actually care about instead.

Any per-entity side-table keyed by `(World, eid)` (`PhysicsBody`'s callback/handle side-table, `VisualScriptState`'s evaluation-scope side-table, `Coroutines.ts`'s scheduled coroutines) needs an explicit `clear(world, eid)` called from `Scene.destroy()`, not just `WeakMap`'s eventual GC once the whole `World` is dropped — that GC never happens for a pooled entity's slot, since the `World` stays alive for the whole scene. Without this, a prefab-pooled entity's reused bitECS id would inherit the previous occupant's stale side-table entries.

### Prefab `.d.ts` codegen lives in toolchain, not the engine

`generatePrefabTypes` (`packages/toolchain/src/prefabCodegen.ts`) reads a project's `.prefab.json` files plus the project's real, registered `ComponentDef`s and emits a `.d.ts` string declaring one `PrefabDef<{...}>`-typed `declare const` per prefab. It lives in `packages/toolchain`, not the engine, because it never touches a `Scene`/`World` — it's pure offline codegen, the same "reads source files, emits a sibling file" shape as the GMS2 importer, not a runtime capability. The engine side (`SceneFile.ts`) owns the complementary runtime half — parsing that same prefab/scene JSON into a `PrefabDef` a live `Scene` can actually `spawn()` — and both sides import the same `ComponentLookup`/`PrefabFile` shapes from `@emptysock/engine` so the two halves can't drift apart on what a field means. `PrefabDef<T>` itself carries an unused, `@internal` `__props?: T` phantom field purely so `Scene.spawn<T>(prefab: PrefabDef<T>, props?: Partial<T>)` can infer `T` from whichever prefab value is passed — `definePrefab` leaves `T` at its `SerializableRecord` default for hand-authored prefabs, and `generatePrefabTypes`'s emitted `declare const` is what actually pins `T` to a concrete shape for a JSON-authored one. Wiring `generatePrefabTypes` into a real `packages/toolchain/src/cli.ts` build command is done — `emptysock-toolchain codegen-prefabs <project-dir> [--out <path>] [--components <modules...>]` (the command itself thin, its actual logic in `prefabCodegenCli.ts`'s `runCodegenPrefabs()` so it's testable without spawning the built `dist/cli.js` binary) recursively finds every `*.prefab.json` under `<project-dir>` (skipping `node_modules`/`dist`), builds a `ComponentLookup` seeded from every `ComponentDef` `@emptysock/engine` exports plus whatever `ComponentDef`s the optional `--components` module paths export (a real game's own custom components live in the game's own compiled JS, which the CLI can't discover on its own — the caller names those modules explicitly), and writes the generated `.d.ts` to `<project-dir>/prefabs.generated.d.ts` by default. Wiring it into an IDE auto-save hook is still a real, separate, not-yet-started follow-up — not required for the CLI build command to count as done.

### Input snapshot: frozen by copy, not by timing

`InputManager.snapshot()` (called once, first, by `Game.update()`) freezes input by making an actual copy — `keys: input.snapshotKeys()` (a fresh `Map`), a fresh `Map` of every gamepad's state, and the current `touches` array — into a private `_frozen` object. `isDown()`/`keyboard`/`gamepad()`/`touches` all read only `_frozen`, never the live `InputSystem`/`GamepadSystem` underneath. This matters because `InputSystem`'s own `_keys` map is mutated live by DOM event listeners between synchronous ticks of the event loop — relying on "JS is single-threaded, so nothing can mutate it mid-`update()`" would happen to work for real device events, but it would silently break the instant anything called `InputSystem`'s internals directly instead of through the frozen copy. Copy-based freezing makes the guarantee independent of _how_ something tries to change input mid-frame, not just "how fast the OS can deliver an event".

Headless/testing input injection is non-DOM on purpose: `InputSystem.simulateKeyDown(code)`/`simulateKeyUp(code)` write directly to the internal key map — no `KeyboardEvent`, no `window`, no jsdom dependency — so the engine's Node/Vitest path can exercise real action-mapping and freeze-per-frame behavior without a DOM. `Game` never calls `InputManager.attach()` itself; only host bootstrap code (browser preview shell, Tauri WebView entry point) does, which is what keeps a headless `Game` from touching `window` at all.

### Audio stays a Game-owned singleton, not a per-entity component

`AudioSystem` (Howler-backed) has no per-entity audio-emitter component anywhere — games hold a reference to one `AudioSystem` instance and call `.play(id)` on it directly. `Game.ts` constructs one `AudioSystem` in its constructor (`game.audio`, also handed through `SceneLifecycle.audio` for convenience) and never recreates or destroys it on `loadScene`/`unloadScene`, since music commonly needs to keep playing across a scene transition and the engine has no automatic per-scene audio teardown. A game that wants scene-scoped sound (stop this scene's sfx/music on unload) does it explicitly from that scene's own `onUnload` (e.g. `audio.stop(id)` or `audio.unloadAll()`).

### Deterministic Rapier build is imported via a non-literal specifier

`PhysicsSystem.init()`/`PhysicsSystem3D.init()` choose between `@dimforge/rapier{2,3}d-compat` and the `-deterministic-compat` build with `await import(moduleName)` where `moduleName` is a runtime string, not a literal. A literal `import("@dimforge/rapier2d-deterministic-compat")` would make TypeScript (and any bundler resolving imports at build time) treat the deterministic build as a hard dependency of `@emptysock/engine`, which defeats the point of it being an `optionalDependency` (most games never install it and shouldn't pay for it, including at install/bundle time). Keep this non-literal if the deterministic swap logic ever moves.

A real, separate, still-open gap: once `apps/ide`'s runtime bundler externalizes `@dimforge/rapier2d-compat` (necessarily — it's a real optional native/WASM dependency, not something to actually bundle into the IIFE), `PhysicsSystem.init()`'s `await import(moduleName)` becomes a genuine bare-specifier dynamic `import()` at runtime with no import map to resolve it. This is a browser platform limitation, not a bundler configuration mistake — physics has likely never worked in the IDE's browser preview, full stop. Not fixed; needs an import-map entry mapping the bare specifier to a real ESM build of rapier's WASM wrapper, or a small runtime shim `apps/ide` registers before the game module loads, in a dedicated future pass. The default new-project boilerplate sidesteps this by passing `manageLifecycle: false` to `loadScene()` (a sprite-only starter has no physics bodies to justify eating this cost anyway).

### `RenderPipeline` tracks sprites per-`Scene`, not by raw entity id

`Game` can have several live scenes at once — the main scene plus any `loadOverlay()`-ed overlays — and each one owns its own bitECS `World`, whose entity ids independently start from 0. That means the main scene's entity `eid 3` and an overlay's entity `eid 3` are two different entities that happen to share a number. `RenderPipeline.ts` keys its sprite/texture-path tracking per `Scene` (`Map<Scene, SceneTracking>`) to avoid aliasing them — the same "never index by a raw entity id without first scoping by which world it belongs to" rule `ComponentRegistry` and `PhysicsBody`'s callback side-table already follow, just scoped by `Scene` instead of `World` since `RenderPipeline` is an external system reaching in, not a component module. Overlay sprites each get one flat, self-sorting `Container` appended to the stage after the main scene's layer containers, which is enough for draw-order-within-an-overlay without needing cross-container named layers.

That per-`Scene` scoping covers the _main_ scene too, not just overlays: `Game.unloadScene()`/`loadScene()` swap in a brand new `Scene` (a new bitECS `World`, entity ids starting at 0 again), so a single flat tracking object reused across that swap would alias the old scene's leftover Pixi sprites onto the new scene's same-numbered entities, and leave the old sprites themselves never destroyed. `_syncMain` tracks which `Scene` its tracking currently belongs to and, the moment a _different_ `Scene` object is passed in, fully disposes the previous one's tracking (`_releaseMain`, sharing the exact same per-sprite teardown `releaseOverlay`/`_pruneOverlays` already use for overlays) before starting fresh.

### `RenderPipeline` mounts a tilemap through a structural interface, not `@emptysock/tilemap`'s `Tilemap`

`RenderPipeline` stays in the core engine, since every game needs to render, not just ones with tile levels, so it cannot import `Tilemap` without making `@emptysock/engine` depend on the very module package that's supposed to depend on it. `RenderPipeline.ts` declares `TileLayerSource`, a plain structural interface covering only the `{ data: { tileWidth, tileHeight, rows, cols, tileset, layers } }` shape `mountTilemap()` actually reads; `@emptysock/tilemap`'s `Tilemap` satisfies it without either package importing the other, the same "engine depends on the interface, never a concrete implementation" pattern as `StorageAdapter`. A consequence: tests that need both a real `RenderPipeline` and a real `Tilemap` together (verifying tiles actually get mounted) live in `packages/tilemap/src/__tests__/RenderPipelineIntegration.test.ts`, since `@emptysock/tilemap` is the package that already depends on both.

### `Game.attachRenderer` takes a structural interface, not the concrete `RenderPipeline`

`Game.ts` defines `SceneRenderer` (`renderFrame(main, overlays)`) as a plain interface and never imports `RenderPipeline.ts`, which in turn imports `pixi.js` and returns `HTMLCanvasElement`. `Game.ts` has to keep running under the headless testing harness in plain Node with zero DOM/Pixi involvement (the engine-environment-boundary rule), so it can only depend on the shape a renderer has, never a concrete Pixi-backed one. `Game.update()`'s render step is gated on both "a renderer is attached" and "this scene wasn't loaded with `headless: true`" — belt-and-suspenders, since a `HeadlessGame` never calls `attachRenderer` at all, but the second check means it stays safe even if something did.

### Visual script compilation: per-node cases, not an interpreter

`VisualScriptSystem`'s `compileVisualScriptGraph` turns a `VisualScriptGraph` into a JS module string via `new Function("module", "exports", "console", source)`, not a bundler/transpile step, so it can compile and load in one call inside the engine package with zero new build tooling. The emitted code is a `switch` inside a `while (__next !== undefined)` loop keyed on node id, not straight-line code, because a `VisualScriptGraph` can legally contain a cycle and straight-line generated code cannot represent one. This is compiled output, not an interpreter: each `case` is the one specific statement for that one node with its field values baked in as literals at compile time (`ctx.variables.setVar(1, 5)`, never a generic `execute(node)` call reading `node.kind` at runtime).

The graph itself is treated as shared, immutable data, not per-entity component state — production ECS engines (Unity DOTS's `EntitiesBT`/`DOTS-BehaviorTree`, Bevy's `bevy_behavior`) converge on the same shape. Two entities running the same authored graph reference the same `graphId`, never a duplicated copy of `nodes`/`connections` sitting in bitECS's own parallel arrays. `VisualScriptState` (the component) is deliberately tiny — one field, `graphId: string` — and `registerVisualScriptGraph`/`getVisualScriptGraph`/`unregisterVisualScriptGraph` (`components/VisualScript.ts`) hold the real `VisualScriptGraph` data in a module-level registry keyed by that id, the same "shared static data keyed by id" pattern `@emptysock/network`'s `NetworkedFields` side-map and `TilemapSystem`'s tilemap registry both already use. Many entities running the same authored graph share one `graphId` string and, via `VisualScriptSystem`'s per-`graphId` compiled-module cache, one compiled function.

The per-entity evaluation scope (a graph run's transient `outputKey -> number` bindings) is genuinely per-entity, mutable, non-serializable runtime state — it cannot live on `VisualScriptState` itself, which must stay `Serializable`. It lives in a `WeakMap<World, Map<eid, Map<string, number>>>` side-table instead (`getVisualScriptScope`/`clearVisualScriptScope`), the same shape `PhysicsBody`'s callback side-table already uses. `Scene.destroy()` calls `clearVisualScriptScope` alongside `clearPhysicsBody`/`clearCoroutines` for the same pooled-id-reuse reason those two already require.

`VisualScriptSystem` takes an optional shared `VariableStore`/`ActorSystem` once, at construction — matching `SceneLifecycle`'s "one instance per scene, shared by whatever reads it" convention (see "VNSystem and MapEventSystem default to an isolated VariableStore" below): pass `ctx.variables`/`ctx.actors` from a scene's `onLoad` to share state with the rest of the game, or leave the constructor defaults for an isolated instance. `update(scene)`/`fireEvent(scene, eventType)` drive every `VisualScriptState` entity via `scene.each()`.

The Visual Script Editor panel's own UI (`apps/ide`'s `visual-script/*.tsx`, `logicScriptStore.ts`) authors the `VisualScriptGraph` shape directly (`VSNode`/`VSConnection`/`VisualScriptGraphBuilder`, all exported from `@emptysock/engine`) — wiring the panel to call `registerVisualScriptGraph`/emit `VisualScriptState` onto a live entity for its own preview is separate, not-yet-started follow-up work.

### WidgetTree: bitECS relations for structure, yoga-layout for measure/arrange, three real gotchas

`ui/WidgetTree.ts` is the first real consumer of bitECS's relations/hierarchy API in this codebase, and of `yoga-layout`. Three things about actually using them are non-obvious enough to have cost real debugging time:

1. **`queryHierarchy` is not a public bitecs@0.4.0 export.** It exists as a real internal function, but the package's own `index.d.ts` only re-exports `getHierarchyDepth`/`getMaxHierarchyDepth` from its `Hierarchy` module — not `queryHierarchy`/`queryHierarchyDepth`. The documented, exported way to get the same parent-before-child depth-sorted traversal is `query(world, [...components, Hierarchy(relation)])`; `Cascade` is a literal alias for `Hierarchy` in this version (`var Cascade = Hierarchy`), not a distinct traversal mode. `WidgetTree.orderedWidgets()` is the one place that does this correctly — route any future hierarchy-ordered query through it (or the same pattern) rather than trying to import `queryHierarchy` directly, which doesn't exist at the public API surface.
2. **A `query()`/`Hierarchy()` term must be the real bitECS-registered store, not the `ComponentDef`.** `entity.add(SomeComponent)`/`entity.get(SomeComponent)` take the plain `ComponentDef` object, but bitECS's own `query()` needs the actual per-`World` store object `ComponentRegistry.ensure(world, def)` returns — passing the `ComponentDef` directly compiles fine and silently matches zero entities, no error. `WidgetTree.orderedWidgets()` calls `componentRegistry.ensure()` itself so nothing else has to remember this.
3. **`Hierarchy`/`Cascade` query results are cached per-relation, invalidated only by a relation pair changing — not by destroying the underlying entity.** Destroying a childless widget and re-running a `Hierarchy()`-ordered query can still return its now-stale eid, and `getRelationTargets` throws given one. `orderedWidgets()` filters every result through `entityExists()` before returning it — any other code building a hierarchy-ordered query over a relation that entities can be destroyed out from under needs the same defensive filter.

Separately: `yoga-layout@3.2.1`'s async WASM init (`loadYoga()`) is imported from the package's `yoga-layout/load` subpath, not its default `.` entry — the default entry's own module-level side effects for auto-loading the WASM synchronously are undocumented magic this codebase deliberately avoids; `./load` re-exports the same plain enum constants (`FlexDirection`, `Edge`, `Gutter`, …) plus an explicit `loadYoga(): Promise<Yoga>` with no ambiguity about when the WASM actually loads. The WASM binary is embedded as base64 directly in the npm package (no runtime fetch), which is what makes `WidgetTree.init()` safe to await under the headless Node/Vitest testing harness with zero DOM.

`LayoutStyle.flexDirection`'s `0`/`1` ordinals are this component's own, deliberately not yoga's real `FlexDirection` enum values (`Column = 0`, `Row = 2`, with reverse variants at 1/3) — keeping the component's schema value independent of whichever layout library sits underneath it, translated by `WidgetTree`'s adapter. `LayoutStyle.width`/`.height` use `-1` as an "auto" sentinel (maps to yoga's `setWidthAuto()`/`setHeightAuto()`) rather than a second boolean pair per axis, since `Serializable` already allows a plain number field and every other field here is one.

`LayoutStyle.positionType: 1` opts a widget out of the parent's flex flow entirely, positioned by `left`/`top` alone (yoga's `PositionType.Absolute`) — the shape a fixed-position HUD overlay or an anchored UI-editor widget needs, independent of any parent's flex flow. `0` (the default) is ordinary flex-flow layout.

### `ui/UISystem.ts`: widget state lives on components, not event-emitter callbacks

`UISystem` covers hit-testing, press/drag/click dispatch with a fixed drag threshold, and hover, against `WidgetTree`'s entity-per-widget tree and the widget-kind components in `components/Widgets.ts` (`Label`, `PanelStyle`, `ButtonState`, `Checkbox`, `Slider`, `Progress`, `ImageWidget`). There is no `.on("click", cb)` event emitter. A `Checkbox`'s `checked` field flips in place when `UISystem` resolves a click; a `Slider`'s `value` updates in place while being dragged; a `ButtonState`'s `state` (0 normal / 1 hover / 2 pressed) is written by pointer dispatch every frame. Game code reads these by polling the component each frame, the same "state lives in the component, game code reads it" style `VisualScriptState`/`PhysicsBody` already use — there is no ECS-native equivalent of an event bus to hang a callback off of, and inventing one just for widgets would be a second, parallel notification mechanism alongside the engine's actual query-driven update model. A panel-shaped widget that needs a click (a dialogue box advancing on click, say) does its own hit-test against the widget's `Layout` box rather than depending on `UISystem` to dispatch one (see `@emptysock/vn`'s `VNTextbox.handlePointerDown()` for a real example).

Per-widget animation (`fadeIn`/`slideIn`/`pop`/`shake`) and anchor resolution outside the placement-editor use case are real, tracked gaps, not silently dropped.

`ImageWidget` loads and caches its source for real: `UISystem`'s `_renderImage()` resolves `ImageWidget.src` through an `ImageLoader` (`(path) => Promise<Texture>`, defaulting to pixi's `Assets.load` — the same loader `RenderPipeline`'s `TextureLoader` wraps), cached by path in a `Map<string, ImageCacheEntry>` shared across every widget instance so the same path is loaded once, not once per widget or once per frame. `IUIRenderer.drawImage()` takes a plain `object`, not a DOM image type, so `_renderImage()` passes `texture.source.resource` (pixi's own underlying drawable — an `ImageBitmap`/`HTMLImageElement`/canvas depending on host and asset type) straight through, keeping this file free of any DOM image import. The grey placeholder box remains the fallback for "no source set", "still loading", and "failed to load" — it stops being drawn only once a source has actually resolved to a loaded texture. `UISystem.ts` is one of the files the root `eslint.config.mjs` allowlists to import `pixi.js` directly (alongside `RenderPipeline.ts`/`RenderSystem.ts`/etc.), since it's a real wrapper around pixi, not game code.

`ui/Anchor.ts`'s `resolveAnchoredPosition(anchor, x, y, w, h, containerW, containerH)` is the nine-point anchor math (`"top-left"` through `"bottom-right"`) that resolves a designer-authored offset against a known viewport/canvas size into an absolute `LayoutStyle.left`/`.top` pair (with `positionType: 1`). It's a pure function, not a component or a system — apps/ide's UI Placement Editor is its main consumer today.

`CGGallery`/`DebugOverlaySystem` both need a settings-blob persistence story and both take a `StorageAdapter` (`get`/`set`/`delete`/`listKeys`) directly, not `SaveSystem` — `SaveSystem` serializes a live `Scene`'s entities/components, and a CG-unlock flag set or a debug overlay's own state isn't per-entity component data, so `SaveSystem`'s `Scene`/`ComponentDef`-bound API is the wrong shape for it regardless of how small the blob is. The rule going forward: a `Game`-level settings/flags blob that isn't tied to one scene's live entities takes a `StorageAdapter` directly; only real per-entity save data goes through `SaveSystem`.

### ParticleEmitter renders through a real pixi ParticleContainer, rebuilt from scratch every frame

`ParticleEmitter` (`systems/ParticleSystem.ts`) is a pure, renderer-agnostic simulation with zero pixi dependency. `RenderPipeline.mountParticles(emitter, layerName?)`/`unmountParticles(emitter)` wire it into actual gameplay rendering: one pixi core `ParticleContainer` per mounted emitter (`ParticleContainer`/`Particle` are core pixi.js exports — no new dependency), and `RenderPipeline.renderFrame()` calls a private `_syncParticles()` every frame that does `container.removeParticles()` then rebuilds the whole list from `emitter.getParticles()` — it does not diff or reuse `Particle` objects across frames. This is a deliberate tradeoff (simplicity over per-frame allocation cost); revisit it if particle counts in a real game ever become a measured bottleneck. An emitter with no `options.texture` set (the default is `""`) renders with `Texture.WHITE` rather than nothing, so a particle effect mounted before its real texture is ready is still visible. `ParticleEmitterOptions.sizeWiggle`/`.speedWiggle`/`.dirWiggle` are real per-step random fluctuations (a fresh offset drawn every step, not a fixed per-particle phase) `ParticleEmitter.update()` applies on top of the deterministic scale/velocity curve — the compat layer's `part_type_size`/`part_type_speed`/`part_type_direction` `*_wiggle` parameters translate straight onto them. `ParticleEmitterOptions.blendMode` (`"normal"`/`"add"`) is a real per-container pixi `blendMode`, set once at `mountParticles()` time — GameMaker's `part_type_blend` translates straight onto it, since pixi batches every particle in one `ParticleContainer` under a single blend mode, matching GameMaker's own per-type (not per-particle) blend setting.

### `apps/ide` bundles and types exactly one engine surface, and the live Inspector bridge is real

`apps/ide/engine-runtime.build.mjs` bundles `@emptysock/engine`'s one export surface as `window.EmptySockEngine` for the preview iframe, and `apps/ide/vite.config.ts`'s `engineTypesPlugin` types Monaco's Code editor against the same `dist-types/index.d.ts`. Keeping these two in sync matters: a mismatch would let a game typecheck against one API while running a different one at runtime. `engine-runtime.build.mjs` also externalizes `@dimforge/rapier{2,3}d-deterministic-compat` alongside the non-deterministic builds — Rolldown resolves both branches of `PhysicsSystem`'s runtime `moduleName` ternary at build time and fails hard on a genuinely-uninstalled optional dependency otherwise.

The default new-project boilerplate (`ideStore.ts`'s `INITIAL_CODE`) is `defineScene`, `scene.spawn()`, `entity.add(Component, props)`, `RenderPipeline`/`game.attachRenderer()`, a `requestAnimationFrame` loop. `RenderPipeline.init()` must be awaited before `.canvas`/`attachRenderer()` are usable (throws "RenderSystem not initialized" otherwise); the boilerplate does this. It also passes `manageLifecycle: false` to `loadScene()` — see "Deterministic Rapier build" above for why.

The live Inspector bridge is real and verified end to end, not just typechecked. `apps/ide/src/services/PlayRunner.ts`'s iframe bootstrap script polls `window.EmptySockEngine.Game.instances` (a pure, DOM-free static `Set<Game>` every `Game` constructor call adds itself to — the mechanism that lets a preview host find a `Game` it never constructed, without game code opting in to anything IDE-specific), constructs/attaches a `QueryChannel` to whichever `Game`'s `currentScene` it finds, and relays `es:query`/`es:query-result` over `postMessage`. `EngineChannel.ts` (the IDE-side transport) is a request/response `query<T>(EngineQuery): Promise<EngineQueryResult<T>>`. `summaryToSnapshot()` converts `QueryChannel.EntitySummary`'s numeric entity ids and optional `Meta`/`Transform`-derived fields into the `EntitySnapshot` shape `SceneInspector.tsx`/`EntityProperties.tsx` render; edits go through `QueryChannel`'s `setComponent` query kind, which merges a patch into a component's live fields through the same proxy `getComponent`/`listEntities` already read from.

`QueryChannel` doesn't need `registerComponents(...)` called with a hardcoded list before it can see anything: `ComponentRegistry.registeredComponents(world): ComponentDef[]` returns every component name at least one live entity has used, in registration order, scoped per-`World` like everything else in that class, and `QueryChannel._resolveComponents()`/`_resolveComponent()` merge manually-registered defs with whatever the registry has actually observed live. This is what makes the bridge work against a game whose component set was never enumerated up front.

Verified by extracting `PlayRunner.ts`'s real `buildIframeHtml()` template and bundling `EngineChannel.ts` standalone into a two-window headless Chromium harness — a real parent page and a real iframe running the real generated engine bundle and the real default-project boilerplate — confirming `listEntities` found both seeded entities, `setComponent` wrote through to the live entity, and a follow-up `getComponent` read the new value back.

### `Tilemap`'s root entity is spawned lazily by `loadInto()`, not eagerly by `register()`

`@emptysock/tilemap`'s `TilemapSystem.register(data)` is called before any `Scene` necessarily exists (a project's tilemaps are typically registered once at startup, then loaded into whichever scene needs them later) — but an `Entity` cannot exist without a real bitECS `World` to belong to. `Tilemap.entity` is therefore `null` until `TilemapSystem.loadInto(scene, name)` actually calls `scene.spawn()` and binds the result via the package-internal `_bindEntity()` — `register()` only ever constructs the map's plain data (`width`/`height`/`getLayer()`/`asGrid()`/`tileAt()` all work off `data` alone, no entity needed). Nothing outside `TilemapSystem.ts` itself reads `.entity` directly — `RenderPipeline.mountTilemap()` only needs the structural `TileLayerSource` shape (`{ data: {...} }`), never the entity. Any future system that wants to "prepare data before a scene exists, spawn a real entity once one does" should follow the same shape: a nullable entity field, set once by whichever method actually receives a live `Scene`.

### `@emptysock/toolchain`'s GMS2 codegen only has one live implementation per asset kind

`buildObjectBehavior()`/`buildObjectPrefabJSON()` (`gms2-codegen.ts`) is the one canonical codegen path `importGMS2Project` actually calls. A module being re-exported from `packages/toolchain/src/index.ts` is not by itself evidence it's live — grep for real callers inside `gms2-import.ts` (the one real entry point) before trusting an export list.

### GitPanel shells out to git via a plain Tauri command, not the shell plugin

`GitPanel.tsx` calls `run_git(project_dir, args)`, a single Tauri command in `lib.rs` that does a plain `std::process::Command::new("git").current_dir(project_dir).args(args).output()` — the same pattern `open_in_vscode`/`export_game` use. This needs no shell-execute scope configuration in `capabilities/default.json`, unlike the shell plugin's scoped-execute allowlist. `args` is a real `Vec<String>` handed straight to `Command::args()`, never concatenated into a shell string, so a commit message or file path containing shell metacharacters can't break out of the intended argv. One generic passthrough (rather than one Tauri command per git subcommand) is deliberate: `GitPanel` already assembles the exact argv it wants for each operation (status/diff/add/reset/commit/push/log), so a second Rust-side API re-encoding the same subcommands would just be a parallel thing to keep in sync for no benefit.

### "Open in VS Code" has no real path in browser preview

`VsCodeService.openInVsCode()` shells out to `code <path>` via a Tauri command (`open_in_vscode` in `lib.rs`, plain `std::process::Command`) on desktop. In the browser preview there is no equivalent: the File System Access API's `FileSystemDirectoryHandle` (what `ProjectService.openDirectoryBrowser` gets from `showDirectoryPicker()`) exposes only a `name`, never a real OS path, and there is no browser API that recovers one. The `vscode://file/<absolute-path>` URI scheme has nothing to open in browser-preview mode without one. `openInVsCodeBrowser()` still checks for a real absolute path (so a future browser API or host wrapper isn't silently ignored) but in the browser-preview mode this repo ships today that check always fails, and the button says so plainly rather than pretending the click did something.

### Inspector schema lookup is keyed by componentName string, mirroring the field mismatch it has to tolerate

`defineComponent`'s optional `schema` is a plain object attached to the returned `ComponentDef`, keyed by field name — no decorators, no separate registry. `apps/ide`'s `EntityProperties.tsx` reads it via a small `componentName -> ComponentInspectorMeta` lookup map (`V2_COMPONENT_METADATA`) built once from the component modules it imports (`Transform`, `Sprite`, `PhysicsBody`), not by importing every component module the IDE might ever encounter. That one map covers both each component's `.schema` and its inspector dot color, so there's only one place to update per component. This matters because the Inspector's `component.type` string (editor state, sourced from the live engine bridge or the editor's own entity list) is not guaranteed to line up 1:1 with a schema entry, and even a schema'd component may have fields the schema doesn't cover (`PhysicsBody`'s `position`/`velocity`/handle fields are deliberately unlisted). Both cases — component not in the map, or field not in that component's schema object — must resolve to the same fallback: the pre-existing raw per-field text editor and the default muted dot color, not an error or a blank control. `ComponentSection` checks `schema?.[key]` per field, so a schema doesn't need to be all-or-nothing for a component to render correctly. If a future pass wants the Inspector to reflect _every_ registered component's schema instead of a hardcoded few, don't hand-import each one here — that's the moment to add a `componentRegistry`-driven lookup (`ComponentRegistry.ts` already tracks defs per world) rather than growing this file's import list indefinitely.

### MCP server has no 3D physics tool

`physics_raycast_3d` is listed in the emptysock-mcp tool registry but explicitly throws "not implemented", and its test asserts that behaviour. Do not implement it without a Rapier3D WASM build available server-side — the engine's 3D physics runs in the browser WASM context, not in Node.

### QueryChannel: transport-agnostic, and errors instead of fabricated empty results

`QueryChannel` (`bridge/QueryChannel.ts`) is the engine-side half of the MCP live bridge — the one place `emptysock-mcp`'s physics/scene/actor/navmesh tools get a real answer instead of a stub. `QueryChannel` never imports a transport: `handle(query)` is a plain synchronous function — whoever owns a live instance (IDE preview host, a dev build's bootstrap code) wires an actual socket/postMessage pipe around it. A query that finds genuinely nothing (`raycast2d` hits nothing, `overlapCircle2d` finds nothing) returns `{ ok: true, data: null }`/`{ ok: true, data: [] }`, which is a different shape from every "there's nothing to even ask" case: `"no-live-instance"` (nothing `attach()`-ed) and `"no-physics-world"` (a `Scene` is attached but its `PhysicsSystem` was never `.init()`-ed) are both explicit `ok: false` errors. Do not collapse any of these three into one "empty" result — an agent consuming a raycast result that reads `hit: null` needs to know whether that means "clear line of sight" or "nothing was actually queried."

Three more query kinds follow the same shape, each with its own reason for existing:

- **`createEntity`** (`scene_create_entity`) spawns a bare `Scene.spawn()` entity, `entity.add()`s each named, already-registered component (defaults only — this is entity creation, not a full prefab spawn), and, if a `tag` was given, writes it into `Meta.name`/`Meta.tags` (adding a `Meta` component if the entity has none) rather than inventing a second, parallel identity concept next to the one `Meta` already established for the Inspector. A component name that doesn't resolve to a registered `ComponentDef` is reported back in `skipped`, not silently dropped or treated as a hard failure — the same "partial success, honestly reported" shape `SaveSystem`'s per-component migration failures use.
- **`actorSendMessage`/`actorBroadcast`/`actorInboxSize`/`actorList`** relay straight to a real `ActorSystem` — it's native to `@emptysock/engine`, so no structural-interface indirection is needed, unlike navmesh below. `ActorSystem`/`Actor` had no public "how many messages are queued" getter before this; `Actor.inboxSize` was added specifically for `actorInboxSize` to read, rather than reaching into the actor's private mailbox array. A `Scene` can legitimately be live with zero actors running (most scenes have none), so a missing `ActorSystem` is its own error code, `"no-actor-system"` — never `"no-live-instance"`, which would wrongly imply nothing is running at all.
- **`navmeshFindPath`/`navmeshNearestNode`** relay to an optional `NavMeshQuerySource` — a narrow structural interface (`findPath`/`nearestNode` only) that `attach()` takes in place of a concrete class, because `NavMeshSystem` lives in `@emptysock/tilemap`, which depends on `@emptysock/engine`, never the other way around. This is the exact same "engine depends on the interface, never a concrete implementation" pattern `RenderPipeline`'s `TileLayerSource` already uses for mounting a `Tilemap` — `@emptysock/tilemap`'s `NavMeshSystem` satisfies `NavMeshQuerySource` structurally, and neither package imports the other. `NavMeshSystem` gained a public `nearestNode(point): Vec2 | null` (previously only a private `_nearestPolygon` existed) specifically to have something real to expose through this interface. A missing navmesh is `"no-navmesh"`, for the same "a live scene can legitimately have none of this running" reason `"no-actor-system"` exists — a scene with no navmesh loaded is normal, not an error.

`attach(scene, physics?, options?)` grew a third, optional `{ actors?, navmesh? }` parameter for these — the existing two-positional-argument call shape (`attach(scene)`, `attach(scene, physics)`) still works unchanged; nothing that already calls `attach()` needed to change. `apps/ide/src/services/PlayRunner.ts`'s preview bootstrap now passes `{ actors: lifecycle.actors }` (the current scene's real, per-scene `ActorSystem` — see "One `ActorSystem` per scene" above) but no `navmesh`: the IDE has no live tilemap/navmesh panel today that exposes a loaded `NavMeshSystem` instance to attach, so `navmeshFindPath`/`navmeshNearestNode` answer `"no-navmesh"` in the preview — the honest answer, not a manufactured one.

### Toolchain CLI export bundles with Rolldown, not esbuild

`packages/toolchain/src/desktopBuild.ts`'s desktop export step (`emptysock-toolchain export --platform windows|mac|linux`) bundles the game's entry point with the real `rolldown` npm package, not `esbuild` and not `@rolldown/browser` (that one is the browser-WASM build; it's what `apps/ide`'s in-browser live-preview build would use if that separate, not-yet-started migration ever happens). The bundling call is factored out as its own `bundleGameEntry()` export so it's testable without a Rust/`cargo tauri` toolchain installed, which the rest of `buildDesktopApp` requires.

Rolldown's build/output options are not a 1:1 rename of esbuild's — two differences that look like regressions but aren't: there is no top-level `drop: ["console"]` or `target: ["es2020"]` build option; the equivalent lives nested under the Oxc-backed minifier as `minify.compress.dropConsole` and `minify.compress.target`, and only takes effect when `minify` is truthy (so `dropConsole` with `minify: false` is a no-op — matches this CLI's own `--minify`/`--drop-console` flags being independent switches, since `dropConsole` is meaningless without minification actually running). Aggressive property mangling is `minify.compress.mangleProps: { include: <RegExp> }` (an object with a required `include` field), not esbuild's bare `mangleProps: /regex/`.

### Shared internal helpers — `internal/scoped.ts` and `internal/fields.ts`

Two tiny cross-cutting helpers live in `packages/engine/src/internal/` specifically so a recurring pattern doesn't get hand-rolled a fifth time. Check here before writing a new per-world/per-scene side-table or a new "write this field into this component's store" loop.

`scoped.ts` exports `getOrCreate(weakMap, key, create)` and `getOrCreateMapEntry(map, key, create)` — the "look up by key, or create and store a fresh value" check that `ComponentRegistry.ts`'s per-`World` registry, `components/PhysicsBody.ts`'s per-`World` callback/handle side-table, and `RenderPipeline.ts`'s per-`Scene` sprite tracking and overlay containers all need. A future side-table scoped by `World` or `Scene` (or any other object key) should use one of these instead of re-writing the same four-line null check.

`fields.ts` exports `setField(store, field, index, value)` and `setFields(store, index, values)` — "write field F at index I into a component's parallel-array store, growing the array if this is the first write to that field." `Entity.add()`'s defaults/overrides loops, `createComponentProxy`'s setter trap (also in `Entity.ts`), and `ComponentRegistry.ensure()`'s shape-change reset path all route through this. Any new code that writes directly into a `Record<string, unknown[]>` component store (rather than going through `entity.get()`/`entity.add()`) should use `setField`/`setFields`, not reimplement the grow-on-first-write check inline.

### LightingSystem: real point-light falloff, and real shadow-casting occlusion

`LightingSystem` (`systems/LightingSystem.ts`) collects every enabled `LightSource` (a point light with `radius`/`colour`/`intensity`/`falloff`, position read from `Transform` plus an offset, same convention `Sprite`/`PhysicsBody` use) into a plain, framework-agnostic `LightSample[]`; `RenderSystem.syncLighting()` turns that list into pixel output — a real offscreen lightmap `RenderTexture` built from concentric additively-blended `Graphics` circles per light, composited over the scene via `pixi-filters`' real `SimpleLightmapFilter` (see that method's own doc comment for why this, not a hand-rolled multi-light shader, is the library-level primitive this system is built on).

**Shadow-casting is real, not aspirational.** A `LightSource` on one side of a wall no longer illuminates straight through it — the "dark cave with torches" case this system exists for. `components/LightOccluder.ts` marks an entity as a light-blocker: a plain axis-aligned box (`width`/`height`, positioned via `Transform` + offset, `enabled` toggle — the same shape `LightSource` itself already uses, deliberately, so the two components read as obvious siblings). This is a dedicated component, not a reuse of `Meta.solid` — `Meta.solid` is GameMaker's collision-query flag with no geometry of its own (`place_meeting`/`place_free` instead derive an AABB from `spriteHalfExtents()`), so a real box a light can actually cast a shadow from has nowhere to live on `Meta` regardless; once a dedicated component is needed for the geometry anyway, keeping "blocks light" as its own concern (rather than folding it into `Meta.solid`) also keeps two genuinely-different-in-general properties honestly independent — an iron gate can be solid for collision and translucent to light, a magic ward can block light with nothing solid to collide with. An ordinary wall that should do both simply carries both components on the same entity, the ordinary ECS answer.

**The algorithm** (`systems/LightOcclusion.ts`, pure geometry, no pixi import — stays inside the engine environment boundary, fully unit-testable under plain Node/Vitest) is the standard "visibility polygon from occluder-segment endpoints" technique: for each light, cast a ray from its centre at the angle of every nearby occluder-segment endpoint (plus a hair before/after each one, so a ray grazing a corner samples both sides of it), find the closest segment intersection along each ray via the standard cross-product ray/segment parametrisation, clipped to the light's own radius (which doubles as its natural far clip), and connect the resulting hit points in angle order into a polygon. Between occluders, extra angle samples evenly spaced around the full circle (`LightingSystemOptions.raySamples`, default 32) keep an unoccluded arc looking like an arc rather than a straight polygon chord. `LightOcclusion.test.ts` and `LightingSystem.test.ts` assert this against real, hand-worked-out geometry (a point directly behind a wall segment is not in the resulting polygon; a point beside it is; a light close enough to a short wall illuminates past its ends) via a real point-in-polygon check, not "renders without throwing".

**Spatial culling, and the honest remaining perf caveat.** `LightingSystem.collectLights()` gathers every enabled `LightOccluder` once per call (not once per light), then per light runs `boxWithinReach()` — an O(1) AABB-vs-circle distance test — before any ray work, so a wall on the far side of the level never enters a torch's ray-casting pass. Worst case is still `O(lights × occluders × rays)`, the same shape `RenderSystem.renderMultiCamera()`'s own doc comment already names for its N-render-pass cost; for the "5-10 torches, dozens of wall segments" dungeon scale this system targets, that's a few thousand cheap ray/segment tests per frame — a scene leaning on hundreds of simultaneously-occluded lights still needs real device profiling before shipping, the same honest caveat this codebase's other N-pass rendering features already carry rather than pretending is free.

**Rendering side**: `LightSample.visibility` is `null` when no occluder was within a light's radius — the common case — which is what keeps an occluder-free scene byte-for-byte identical to the pre-occlusion implementation: `RenderSystem`'s `buildLightGraphics()` renders the ordinary un-masked circular falloff whenever it sees `null`. When `visibility` is a real polygon, `buildLightGraphics()` builds a second `Graphics` filling that polygon and sets it as the light `Graphics`' `.mask` — a genuine pixi geometric mask (not a CSS/filter approximation), in the same local coordinate space, deliberately never added to `_lightMapContainer`'s own display tree (pixi masks against another display object's geometry without requiring it to be in the scene graph, as long as both share the same coordinate space, which they do here).

### PostProcessSystem's layer filters become real pixi Filters, not just CSS strings

`PostProcessSystem.setLayerFilter(layerId, opts)` stores a framework-agnostic `LayerFilterOptions` (a type string plus params) and can render a CSS-string approximation via `cssFilterForLayer()` for a host that draws a layer as a DOM element. `RenderSystem.syncPostProcessLayerFilters(postProcess)` translates those same options into a real PixiJS filter for the actual WebGL/WebGPU-rendered layers: it reads `postProcess.layerFilters` and builds/updates one real `Filter` per layer id via `addLayerShaderFilter()` (an engine-owned side-table, keyed by layer id, the same pattern `PhysicsBody`'s callback side-table uses). The effect-to-library mapping is `blur` → pixi.js core's `BlurFilter`; `brightness`/`contrast`/`saturate`/`hue-rotate`/`invert`/`colour-grade` → pixi.js core's `ColorMatrixFilter` via its chainable convenience methods; `colourblind` → `ColorMatrixFilter` with `PostProcessSystem`'s own `COLOURBLIND_MATRICES` CVD-simulation coefficients embedded directly into the 5x4 matrix (the same coefficients `cssFilterForLayer()`'s SVG `feColorMatrix` fallback already uses, so the two code paths can never visually disagree); `outline` → `pixi-filters@6.1.5`'s `OutlineFilter`. One filter instance is cached per layer id and only rebuilt when that layer's filter _type_ changes — an unchanged type just gets its params re-applied in place — so calling this every frame doesn't reallocate a GPU filter per frame. `CustomShaderFilter`/`LightingSystem` need no equivalent wiring — both already construct a plain pixi `Filter` directly and go through the same pre-existing `addLayerShaderFilter()`.

`addLayerShaderFilter`/`removeLayerShaderFilter` null-coalesce `container.filters` to `[]` before spreading/filtering — PixiJS's own type says `readonly Filter[]` (never `null`/`undefined`), but a freshly constructed `Container` actually has it unset at runtime, so the very first filter ever attached to any layer via either method would otherwise throw. If you hit a PixiJS type claiming something is never null/undefined, verify the runtime behaviour of a fresh instance before trusting the type.

### VNSystem and MapEventSystem default to an isolated VariableStore, not an implicit shared one

`packages/vn/src/VNSystem.ts` and `MapEventSystem.ts` default their `store: VariableStore` constructor parameter to `new VariableStore()` — a fresh, isolated instance. Sharing state across systems is fully supported and easy, but explicit at the call site: pass `ctx.variables` (the same `Game`-owned instance every scene's `onLoad` receives via `SceneLifecycle`) to `new VNSystem(ctx.variables)`/`new MapEventSystem(ctx.variables)` when you want dialogue/map-trigger switches to share state with the rest of the game. Without passing it explicitly, a VN choice gated on switch 12 is fully isolated from an unrelated `variableStore.setSwitch(12, ...)` call anywhere else in the same game — there is no bare importable singleton to accidentally collide on.

### VNTextbox has its own hit-test; there's no per-widget click callback

`@emptysock/vn`'s `VNTextbox` spawns its own widget entities (`PanelStyle`+`Label`, positioned via `LayoutStyle`/`resolveAnchoredPosition`) through the caller's `WidgetTree`, and exposes `handlePointerDown(x, y)` — a hit-test against the panel entity's `Layout` box that advances/skips the dialogue on hit. This mirrors the "ui/UISystem.ts: widget state lives on components" entry above: there's no ECS-native click-callback mechanism to hang the "advance on click" behavior off, so the textbox does its own bounds check rather than depending on one.

### GMS2 transpiler symbol pre-scan: stayed regex-based, real research behind the decision — plus a real double-wrap bug the research surfaced and fixed

Researched (WebSearch, not assumed) whether a real, maintained GML parser/lexer exists that could replace this transpiler's hand-rolled per-file regex passes with a real AST for at least the project-wide symbol pre-scan (`gms2-enums.ts`'s `scanGmlEnums`, the object-name/cross-instance detection the "real cross-instance references" section above documents). Three real candidates found: `@bscotch/gml-parser` (npm, actively published — v1.17.2 at research time, ~8 months old — the maintained successor to Bscotch's own retired Stitch CLI, models a whole GMS2/2.3+ project including structs/statics/constructor methods, real position-tracked AST), `gamemaker-language-parser` (Pizzaandy, Antlr4-generated, WIP Prettier plugin — real but pre-1.0 and tooling-focused, not published as a stable consumable library), and `gml-pegjs` (ThomasHickman, explicitly experimental, unmaintained).

`@bscotch/gml-parser` is the one real, suitable, maintained option. **Decision: do not adopt it this pass, for real reasons, not "no library exists":** (1) it models a whole GameMaker _project_ (its own resource graph, `.yyp` conventions, reference tracking) — a much larger surface than this pass needs, and integrating it correctly would mean either running two independent project-model passes (this importer's own `gms2-*-import.ts` family plus `@bscotch/gml-parser`'s) that have to agree on project state, or replacing this importer's own already-real, already-tested `.yyp`/`.yy` parsing (`gms2-parse.ts`, CLAUDE.md's own extensively-documented quirks list above) with its equivalent — a materially larger, riskier rewrite than "swap the pre-scan." (2) This transpiler is 15+ interdependent regex passes verified end-to-end against a real, full GameMaker project (Freedom Backup) with two full `tsc --noEmit` sweeps' worth of real regressions found and fixed; a pre-scan built on a genuinely different parser (its own tokenizer, its own notion of scope/identifiers) risks disagreeing with what the regex passes downstream already assume about masked strings/comments (`maskGmlStringLiterals`) and identifier boundaries, for a project that already imports and transpiles correctly. (3) No sandboxed way in this pass to add and pin a new npm dependency's exact version against a real end-to-end proof it doesn't regress the existing 409-test toolchain suite — a real, unvalidated risk, not a hypothetical one, and this codebase's own precedent (e.g. the deterministic-Rapier-build entry, the "unvalidated perf-risk rendering path" reasoning in the scene-transition entry above) is to not ship an unvalidated swap when the existing, tested path works. Revisit if a future pass needs true AST-level transforms (the enum/static passes are already closer to that need than the per-line rewrites are) and has room for a real, isolated proof-of-concept against the full Freedom Backup regression suite before landing it.

**What was built instead: closed a real, concrete symbol-table bug the research pass's own re-reading of the pre-scan code surfaced** — not a new hand-written scanner class (the existing `_objectNames`/`_enumNames` module-level sets, `maskGmlStringLiterals`-respecting per-file regex passes, and the dotted-reference/known-name guards documented in the "real cross-instance references" section above were re-read and found structurally sound for every real case in Freedom Backup; inventing a second, parallel scope-tracking mechanism on top of an already-correct one would be exactly the kind of ungrounded rewrite item 1's own research explicitly argues against). The real bug: the implicit-array-variable detection pass (`gms2-transpile.ts`, right before the instance-variable pass) and the pre-existing `[| i]`/`[? key]` ds_list/ds_map accessor rewrite pass could double-fire on the same name — `list[| 0] = 5;` (accessor pass strips `| ` to plain `list[0]`, which the array-var pass then correctly identifies as an undeclared implicit array and wraps in `GmlActions.getGmlArrayVar`) produced a **nested** `getGmlArrayVar(_entity, _ctx, "getGmlArrayVar(_entity, _ctx, "list")")` — because the array-var pass's own three sub-passes (indexed-assignment, indexed-read, bare-whole-array-read) run sequentially against the same progressively-rewritten string, and the third (bare-read) sub-pass re-matched the quoted `"list"` text an earlier sub-pass in the same loop iteration had just inserted. Fixed with a `(?<!_ctx, ")` fixed-length negative lookbehind on all three sub-passes, so a sub-pass never re-matches text a sibling sub-pass in the same loop iteration already generated. A second, related guard (`(?!\s*[|?])` on the array-var detection/read regexes) keeps a genuine ds_list/ds_map accessor on the same name from ever being misidentified as a plain array index in the first place. Both confirmed via a real full-project sweep: 432 → 413 `tsc --noEmit` error lines (this file's last documented count re-verified fresh). Tests: `gms2-transpile.test.ts`'s ds_list `[| i]` accessor test updated to assert the correct (previously double-wrapped, now singly-wrapped) real output.

### GMS2 playability blockers found by the smoke test, fixed for real: per-sprite collision extents, and object inheritance/variable-definitions

The playability smoke test's own honest findings above (`obj_player.x` never moving, `obj_enemy`'s `grv`/`hp`/`has_weapon` reference errors) were two real, previously-undiscovered gaps, both fixed this pass, plus one still-open finding this pass's own investigation surfaced.

**Real per-sprite collision extents.** `Sprite` (`packages/engine/src/components/Sprite.ts`) gained `width`/`height` fields (`0` default = genuinely unknown). `gms2-codegen.ts`'s `buildObjectPrefabJSON` now reads an object's initial sprite's real `.yy` `width`/`height` (already parsed by `convertGms2Sprite`, which already exposed them on `SpriteAsset` — no new parsing needed) and seeds them as `Sprite` overrides. `compat/gmlActions.ts`'s `spriteHalfExtents()` now reads `Sprite.width`/`.height` when both are `> 0`, falling back to the old fixed 16px half-extent (32px square) only when genuinely absent. Researched GameMaker's own collision-mask semantics: sprites can use a non-bbox precise mask, but every real sprite in Freedom Backup uses a plain rectangular mask, so a real-dimensions bounding box is the correctly-scoped fix — a full per-pixel mask system would be over-engineering here. Confirmed via the smoke test: `obj_player`'s real box is 10×29 (was a fixed 32×32), `obj_wall`'s is 32×32 — no longer permanently mismatched.

**Real GameMaker object inheritance and GMS2.3+ Variable Definitions — two genuinely different mechanisms, both real gaps, both now implemented.** Investigating `obj_enemy`'s `grv`/`hp`/`has_weapon` found they are **not** set via inheritance at all (a fresh hypothesis this pass initially assumed and then disproved by reading the real `.yy`) — they're GMS2.3+ "Variable Definitions", a real per-object `.yy` `properties` array of typed instance-variable defaults declared on the object resource itself, never in any `.gml` file. `resolveGmlObjectProperties()` (`gms2-codegen.ts`) walks the real `parentObjectId` chain (root-most first, so a child's own properties override a parent's same-named one — this **is** real inheritance, confirmed via GameMaker's manual's Object Inheritance page: "if the child object does not have an event that the parent has, then it will use the parent's event") and reads `varType: 3` as boolean (`"True"`/`"1"` → `true`), everything else as a number when it parses as one, else a raw string (a value that's itself another property's name as an unevaluated expression — real, observed: `obj_enemy.yy`'s own `hsp` property has the literal value `"walksp"` — is read at face value, not evaluated, an honest narrow gap). The resolved names are seeded into `objectImplicitVars` (so a bare _read_ of `grv`, never _assigned_ in any `.gml` file, is recognised the same as an ordinary implicit instance variable) and emitted as `GmlActions.setGmlVar(...)` calls prepended to the generated `onCreate`, before the transpiled Create body runs — matching GameMaker's real timing.

Separately, real object-inheritance **event fallback** is also now implemented: `buildObjectBehavior`'s `buildMethod` searches the real `parentObjectId` chain (`resolveGmlObjectChain()`) for each event slot in child-to-root order, using the nearest ancestor that actually has that event file when the object itself has none — a generated comment names which ancestor a fallen-back event came from. `event_inherited()` (real, confirmed usage: one real call site, `obj_crate/Draw_0.gml`) is not wired — left as an honest unresolved identifier, the same as other genuinely-unmodelled GML — since it needs the compiled parent function reused _inside_ a child's own override, a harder problem than the no-override case this pass solved; a real, separate, named follow-up.

Confirmed via the smoke test: `obj_enemy`'s `grv`/`hp`/`has_weapon` `ReferenceError`s are gone (all three: `hp` turned out to be a real `obj_pShootable` parent property too, resolved by the same chain walk).

**A separate, real, still-open finding from this pass's own investigation, not fixed here:** with real collision extents in place, `obj_player.x` still does not move under held `vk_right` — re-traced (not still attributed to the old 32×32 box) to `obj_player`'s own Step code reading `key_right` via `obj_input.key_right`, a real cross-instance dotted reference (see the cross-instance-references entry above) that depends on `obj_input`'s own input-polling script (`scr_get_input`) running every Step against a live `obj_input` instance — a real, separate, not-yet-traced gap, left honest rather than guessed at further within this pass's scope. `gms2-playability-smoke.test.ts`'s own comments were updated to reflect this corrected root cause. A minor, separate, unrelated finding from the same run: a bare `noone` value reference (`obj_enemy`'s own `else my_gun = noone;`) is a real, still-unwired GameMaker constant — left open, the same class of gap as the already-documented bare `obj_player`-as-value case.

Full-project `tsc --noEmit` sweep before this pass: 337 error lines (last documented count). After: 344 — a small real increase, from the `noone`/cross-instance gaps above newly surfacing now that `grv`/`has_weapon`/`hp` no longer abort `obj_enemy`'s own event bodies early (previously masked). Full engine (640 tests) and toolchain (410 tests) suites pass. Tests: `packages/toolchain/src/__tests__/gms2-sprite-animation.test.ts` (updated — real `width`/`height` overrides on both a multi-frame and single-frame `Sprite`); `packages/toolchain/src/__tests__/gms2-playability-smoke.test.ts` (updated — corrected root-cause comment).

### GMS2 playability: the `vk_right` movement gap was `Scene.spawn()` never stamping `Meta.name`, not a transpiler bug

The prior pass's own "still-open finding" above (`obj_player.x` never moving under held `vk_right`) was traced to completion, not re-guessed. `scr_get_input`'s codegen and `obj_player`'s `key_right = obj_input.key_right;` -> `getGmlObjectVar(_entity, _ctx, "obj_input", "key_right")` rewrite were both re-verified correct — the real cause was one level deeper: `getGmlObjectVar` resolves its target instance by scanning every live entity's `Meta.name` (see the cross-instance-references entry above), but `Meta.name` was only ever stamped from a prefab's own name by `loadSceneFile()`'s `stampPrefabNameOntoMeta()` — a direct `Scene.spawn(prefab)` call, with no `loadSceneFile()` involved, produced an entity with no resolvable object-type identity at all. This is not a test-only gap: `compat/gmlActions.ts`'s `action_create_object` (the function `instance_create`/`instance_create_layer` both route through) called `ctx.scene.spawn(prefab, { x, y })` directly, the exact same bypass — so **any** real GameMaker project's runtime-spawned singleton object (an input manager spawned once from a controller's Create event, a bullet, a pickup, anything created via `instance_create`/`instance_create_layer` rather than room-placed) got an entity `place_meeting`/`onCollideWith<Type>`/`getGmlObjectVar` could never find by object-type name, silently, forever.

Fixed by exporting `stampPrefabNameOntoMeta` from `SceneFile.ts`/`index.ts` (it was a private, unexported function) and calling it from `action_create_object` right after the real spawn, reusing the one existing implementation rather than duplicating the "if no `Meta`, add one; if `Meta.name` is empty, fill it in; never overwrite an explicit name" logic a second time. `gms2-playability-smoke.test.ts`'s own manual `obj_input` spawn (which bypasses `action_create_object`, since it isn't reached via transpiled GML) now calls the same helper explicitly, matching what a real GML-driven spawn does automatically.

Confirmed via the smoke test with temporary debug logging (removed before finishing): a real run moved the player from `startX 160` to `endX 1752` over 400 frames of held `vk_right` — the test's assertion changed from "finite, unmoved" to `endX > startX + 50`. Vertical movement under gravity is unaffected (still asserted).

Full-project `tsc --noEmit` sweep before this pass: 344 error lines. After: 309. Full engine (640 tests) and toolchain (410 tests) suites pass. Tests: `packages/toolchain/src/__tests__/gms2-playability-smoke.test.ts` (updated — real movement assertion, corrected root-cause comment).

### GMS2 transpiler: two real statement-boundary bugs (`case`/`default` labels, multi-statement brace bodies), `layer_*`/room-layer compat, `id`/`noone` built-ins, and the rest of the sweep's top categories

A fresh, verified real `tsc --noEmit` sweep found 339 error lines (not the ~309 last documented — the codebase had changed since; re-verified fresh per this file's own established rule rather than trusted).

**Two real, previously-undiscovered statement-boundary bugs in the shared assignment-rewrite prefix**, both the same root cause as the pre-existing brace-less-`if` fix (a real GML statement legally starting somewhere other than column 0 that the rewrite passes' `(^[ \t]*|\)[ \t]+)` anchor didn't recognise):

- A compiled switch-dispatch body writing its result inline on the same line as its `case`/`default` label (`case e__VW.Visible: __res = view_set_visible(...); break;`, Freedom Backup's own `__view_set_internal.gml`) was never recognised as a line-start assignment at all — the line literally starts with `case `. `GML_STATEMENT_PREFIX` (the passes' shared prefix, factored out of three near-duplicate inline regexes into one named constant this pass) gained a `case\s[^:\n]*:[ \t]*|default\s*:[ \t]*` alternative.
- A brace body with more than one statement on one physical line (`{ vsp = 0; grav = 0; }`, Freedom Backup's own `obj_moveblock`/`obj_slideblock`) left every statement past the first unrecognised — neither `stmt1;` (after a semicolon) nor `{ stmt` (right after an opening brace) is a real line start. `GML_STATEMENT_PREFIX` gained `;[ \t]*|\{[ \t]*` alternatives. Both alternatives echo their captured prefix back verbatim, so every pre-existing case (real line start, brace-less-`if`) stays byte-identical.
- `identifyGmlImplicitVars`'s own separate `bareAssign` regex (the _detection_ half, not the rewrite passes) gained the matching `case`/`default` optional-prefix alternative — `__res` needed recognising as implicit in the first place, not just correctly rewritten once recognised.

**Real room-layer compat, `compat/gmlLayer.ts` (new, sibling to `gmlCamera.ts`/`gmlInput.ts`).** `layer_exists`/`layer_get_id`/`layer_x`/`layer_y`/`layer_get_x`/`layer_get_y`/`layer_force_draw_depth`/`layer_add_instance`/`layer_sprite_get_id`/`layer_sprite_destroy`, plus the bare `layer` built-in (the calling instance's own creation layer — `gml_current_layer(entity, ctx)`). `LayerSystem` gained `hasLayer()`/`setOffset()`/`getOffset()` (backing `layer_exists`/`layer_x`/`layer_y` for real) and `RenderSystem.syncLayerOffsets()` (a real per-frame pass, called alongside the pre-existing `syncLayerVisibility()`, that writes a named layer's stored offset onto its actual pixi `Container` position — real manual-parallax scrolling, not a stored-and-ignored number). `layer_force_draw_depth` is an honest no-op (`LayerSystem`'s own doc comment already states depth sorting here is always explicit, never implicitly re-sorted, so there is nothing for this GameMaker performance toggle to turn off). `layer_sprite_get_id`/`_destroy` are an honest gap, not a fabrication — GameMaker's "layer element" API (a static decorative sprite placed directly on a room layer in the room editor, no object/event code) is not parsed or carried through this importer's generated `.scene.json` at all (a real, separate, deeper gap in `gms2-room-import.ts`, not something a compat function can close), so `layer_sprite_get_id` returns `undefined` (standing in for `noone`) and `layer_sprite_destroy` is a safe no-op. `GmlActionContext` gained an optional `layers?: LayerSystem` field; `GmsProjectRuntime.buildContext()` wires it from `options.renderer.layers` when a renderer was given. `LayerSystem`/`LAYER`/`LayerConfig`/`LayerSortKey` are now exported from `index.ts` for the first time (a real, separate, previously-undiscovered export gap — nothing outside `packages/engine` could name the type before this).

**GameMaker's `id` built-in** (the calling instance's own instance id — real, common wherever an instance passes a reference to itself, confirmed usage: `layer_add_instance("Tiles", id)`) rewrites to `_entity` — this engine's `Entity` _is_ the calling instance's own identity, the same "alias the real engine-side referent" choice `room`'s bare read already makes for `ctx.currentRoom`.

**`shader_set`/`shader_reset`** (`compat/gmlActions.ts`) are a real, honestly-documented approximation, not a shader compiler (this importer parses no GLSL at all): the single confirmed real use in Freedom Backup (`obj_pShootable`'s hit-flash — `shader_set(sh_white); ...; shader_reset();`) is approximated by tinting the calling entity's `Sprite.tint` white for the draw call's duration and restoring it on reset, regardless of which shader name is actually passed — a real, visible, useful effect for this project's actual real use, honestly not a real shader system.

**`noone` used as a bare value** (`my_gun = noone;`, distinct from `noone` as an object-name _argument_ to `place_meeting`/`collision_*`, which already had a real, working, earlier quoting pass) rewrites to JS `undefined` — placed _after_ that earlier quoting pass in the pipeline specifically so it can never corrupt the identifier that pass still needs to see bare, guarded with `(?<!["'])`/`(?!["'])` so an already-quoted `"noone"` string is never touched a second time.

**Real room-navigation built-ins**: `room_goto_next` (alias for the already-real `action_next_room`), `room_restart` (reloads `ctx.currentRoom` via the already-real `action_another_room`), `room_last` (the last room name in `ctx.roomOrder` — this importer addresses rooms by name, not GameMaker's real numeric index, the same choice `room_exists` already makes), `previous_room` (the room loaded immediately before the current one — `GmsProjectRuntime` now tracks `_previousRoom`, captured right before `_currentRoom` is overwritten on every room load, and threads it into `GmlActionContext.previousRoom`), `room_speed` (an honestly-documented assumed `60`, the same `ASSUMED_STEPS_PER_SECOND` convention `gms2-sprite-import.ts`'s own `playbackSpeedType: 0` conversion already uses — GMS2 rooms carry no per-room speed field in their `.yy` at all, it's a project-wide setting). **A real, confirmed regression this surfaced and fixed**: Freedom Backup's own `obj_player_stats` declares a plain instance variable that happens to share `previous_room`'s exact name (`previous_room = room;`, legally shadowing the read-only GameMaker built-in), and the new bare-read rewrite corrupted that assignment's target into a non-assignable call expression — a real, hard `SyntaxError` the `tsc` sweep could not catch (both sides typecheck) but the playability smoke test's real ES-module-load check did. Fixed with a `(?!\s*=(?!=))` guard on all three room-read rewrites (`room_last`/`previous_room`/`room_speed`), so an assignment-target occurrence is left for the generic implicit-instance-variable pass to handle correctly instead.

**`sprite_width`/`sprite_height`** (the calling instance's own real, scaled sprite dimensions — `Sprite.width`/`.height` times `Transform.scaleX`/`.scaleY`, where `image_xscale`/`image_yscale` actually live on this engine) are real. **`sprite_get_width`/`sprite_get_height`/`sprite_exists`** (an _arbitrary_ sprite asset's raw dimensions/existence by reference — real, confirmed usage: `oTextbox`'s `sprite_get_width(_image)`, where `_image` is a runtime variable) are an honest, documented gap: this compat layer has no general sprite-asset registry reachable from `compat/` at all (a sprite's real pixel dimensions are only ever baked onto one specific entity's own `Sprite` component at import time, never stored anywhere addressable by name/reference alone) — building one is a genuinely new import-time feature, not a same-file fix, so these three honestly return `0`/`0`/`false` rather than a fabricated plausible-looking number.

A real, full-project `tsc --noEmit` sweep before this pass: 339 error lines. After: 288. Full engine (640 tests) and toolchain (410 tests, including the playability smoke test — real player movement and clean `obj_enemy` dispatch reconfirmed, no regression) suites pass. Tests: `gms2-transpile.test.ts` (updated — the `id`-rewrite regression in an existing `show_message` test, now asserting the correct `_entity` output).

Remaining top sweep categories genuinely deferred, with real reasons: cross-instance dotted references through a _local variable_ holding an instance handle (`owner.x`, `owner.image_xscale` in `obj_Egun` — `owner` is a plain local variable, not a known project object-type name, the same already-documented "inst"/"other" class of gap this transpiler cannot resolve without real scope analysis); `bullet_tolerance`/`option`/`stamina`/`maxstamina`/`maxexpr` and similar — not yet individually traced this pass, likely either the same local-variable-reference class or a further object-inheritance Variable Definitions case; `json_encode`/`json_decode`/`base64_encode`/`base64_decode`/`device_mouse_y_to_gui`/`display_set_gui_size`/`window_set_cursor`/`window_get_cursor`/`draw_text_ext`/`draw_text_color`/`draw_roundrect_ext`/`font_get_size`/`get_timer`/`game_restart`/`randomize`/`point_in_circle`/`is_string`/`is_undefined`/`cr_none`/`game_set_speed`/`gamespeed_fps`/`mask_index` — real, individually low-frequency (1-4 occurrences each) built-ins not yet triaged this pass, left for a future sweep rather than rushed.

### GMS2 transpiler: the low-frequency built-in batch from the last pass's deferred list, plus a real, narrow "local variable holds an Entity" dotted-reference mechanism

A fresh, verified real `tsc --noEmit` sweep found 293 error lines (re-verified fresh rather than trusted — the previous pass's own 288 count had already gone slightly stale). This pass closed the low-frequency built-in batch the previous pass's own "Remaining top sweep categories" paragraph named by name, plus implemented a real, narrow version of the "local variable holds an instance reference" dotted-access mechanism the same paragraph's `owner.x` entry called out as needing real scope analysis.

**The named built-in batch is real, not stubbed**, each following this file's own established per-family conventions rather than inventing new ones: `json_encode`/`json_decode` (`compat/gml.ts`) are plain `JSON.stringify`/`JSON.parse` — a GML struct/array literal is already valid JS-object-literal shape (see the GMS2.3+ struct-literal entry above), so no translation is needed, confirmed real, common usage in Freedom Backup's own `scr_save_game.gml`/`scr_load_game.gml` save-file chain. `base64_encode`/`base64_decode` are a genuine dependency-free codec (no `Buffer`, no `btoa`/`atob` — both are Node-only/DOM-only respectively, and the engine-environment-boundary rule forbids assuming either is present), proven by round-trip tests including non-multiple-of-3-length strings. `draw_text_ext`/`draw_text_color`/`draw_roundrect_ext` (`compat/gml.ts`, threaded via their own dedicated `gms2-transpile.ts` rewrite pass rather than joining `THREADED_PURE_FUNCTIONS`/`THREADED_CTX_ONLY`, since all three need `_ctx.drawTarget` the way `draw_text`/`draw_rectangle` already do) are real, honestly-scoped approximations — multi-line splitting on `\n`/`#` with a fixed 16px line height (no font-metrics query exists anywhere in `GmlDrawTarget` to derive a real one from, the same gap `font_get_size` below shares), a flat single-colour draw in place of a 4-corner gradient, and a sharp-cornered rect in place of a rounded one — each drawing something real and visible rather than throwing or silently no-opping. `font_get_size`/`sprite_get_width`-class honest-`0` gaps got one more member: `font_get_size` has no font-asset registry reachable from `compat/` to answer from (same reasoning `sprite_get_width` already documents). `get_timer`/`randomize`/`game_set_speed`/`window_set_cursor`/`window_get_cursor` are each a real, honestly-scoped implementation of a GameMaker built-in this engine cannot fully back (a coarser millisecond-based clock, a documented no-op for an unseedable `Math.random`, a documented no-op for a loop-timing knob this file has no reference to, and a stored-but-not-OS-applied cursor value respectively) — every one of these mirrors an already-established "store/approximate honestly, don't fabricate" pattern from elsewhere in this same file (`application_surface`, `randomize`'s sibling `game_set_speed`, `view_get_surface_id`). `point_in_circle`/`is_string`/`is_undefined` are plain, exact, real geometry/type-check functions with no approximation involved. `gamespeed_fps`/`gamespeed_microseconds`/`cr_default`/`cr_none`/`working_directory` are bare-value constants, threaded through a new `GML_MISC_CONSTANTS` rewrite list (the same plain `\bname\b` → `GmlActions.name` shape `GML_COLOUR_CONSTANTS` already establishes) — `working_directory` is `""`, since `@emptysock/engine` has no filesystem access to report from inside the engine-environment boundary at all, the same class of "no reachable resource" default `font_get_size`'s `0` uses. `display_set_gui_size`/`device_mouse_y_to_gui`/`device_mouse_x_to_gui` (`compat/gmlInput.ts`) are real aliases onto already-existing real mechanisms (`ViewportSystem.setDesignResolution`, the primary-pointer position `mouse_x`/`mouse_y` already read) — `device` is honestly ignored (no per-device pointer index exists in this compat layer, the same already-documented `mouse_x`/`mouse_y` limitation). A real, previously-undiscovered self-nesting bug in `THREADED_PURE_FUNCTIONS`'s own rewrite loop was also found and fixed while wiring `min`/`max` more thoroughly: a single non-recursive `.replace()` pass left a function call nested _inside its own arguments_ (`max(0, x - max(y, z))`, real, confirmed in Freedom Backup's own `obj_sidebars`) with its inner occurrence unrewritten, since `BALANCED_PARENS_TWO_LEVELS` consumes the whole outer call including the inner one's still-bare text — fixed by looping each function's rewrite (bounded to 10 passes) until a pass makes no further change, which converges after exactly one iteration for the overwhelmingly common non-nested case and is a no-op safety net otherwise.

**A real, narrow "local variable holds an Entity" mechanism — implemented, not skipped, per the "if tractable" instruction — but honestly does not close the specific `owner.x` gap it was scoped against.** `compat/gmlCrossInstance.ts` gained `getGmlRefVar`/`setGmlRefVar(entity, ctx, varName, field[, value])`, a real sibling to `getGmlObjectVar`/`setGmlObjectVar` above with the same `x`/`y`-special-cased-else-generic-side-table logic (reused via the same `Transform`/`getGmlVar`/`setGmlVar` calls, not duplicated) but a different resolution mechanism: instead of scanning every live entity's `Meta.name` for an object-_type_ match, it reads `varName`'s own _current value_ through the exact same `getGmlVar` per-`(World, eid)` side-table every bare instance-variable read already uses, and duck-types that value as a real, live `Entity` (`asLiveEntity()` — checking for `Entity`'s own public `.get`/`.isAlive` shape, since `Entity` is a concrete class this file can't `instanceof`-check without importing the class value, only its type). A `varName` that never held a live `Entity` (never assigned, assigned something else, or the instance it pointed to was since destroyed) is a real, honest no-op — `undefined` on read, a console warning on write — the same "no live instance to even ask" convention `getGmlObjectVar`/`setGmlObjectVar` already establish.

`gms2-transpile.ts`'s detection (`localEntityRefs`, the "GML local-variable-held instance references" section) is a real, narrow, same-function text scan — not a full local-variable scope analysis — for one concrete, checkable signal: a plain `name = GmlActions.<fn>(...)` assignment where `<fn>` genuinely returns an `Entity`/`Entity | undefined` (`instance_create_layer`, `action_create_object`/`instance_create`, `instance_place`, `instance_position`). This detection has to run _before_ the generic implicit-instance-variable pass (`identifyGmlImplicitVars`'s rewrite), not after — a real ordering bug found and fixed while implementing this: that pass's own plain-assignment sub-pass rewrites `my_gun = instance_create_layer(...)` into `GmlActions.setGmlVar(_entity, _ctx, "my_gun", GmlActions.instance_create_layer(...))` moments later, after which the `name = GmlActions.<fn>(` shape this detection scans for can no longer be found in `out` at all — `localEntityRefs` is therefore computed once, early, and carried forward as a plain variable to the dotted-rewrite pass that actually uses it, further below.

**A second, real, previously-undiscovered bug found and fixed by writing this feature's own tests, not by re-reading the real corpus** (this specific double-bug never manifests in Freedom Backup itself — see the honest gap below for why — but is a real, general correctness bug regardless): the generic implicit-instance-variable bare-read catch-all had no guard against being _followed_ by a dot at all. `my_gun.hp` (`my_gun` assigned via `instance_create_layer`, then dot-accessed) had its bare `my_gun` token rewrapped into `GmlActions.getGmlVar(...)`, leaving the real `.hp` dangling _after_ the call — `(GmlActions.getGmlVar(...)).hp` still parses (it reads a `.hp` property off `getGmlVar`'s own return value, `undefined` at runtime) rather than throwing a `SyntaxError`, so this silently produced a wrong answer instead of a caught error — a real, more dangerous class of bug than the hard-crash bugs this file's other statement-boundary fixes catch. Fixed with a `(?!\s*\.[A-Za-z_])` exclusion on that catch-all's own regex, so a dot-followed occurrence is left untouched for the dedicated local-ref rewrite pass (further below in the pipeline) to resolve correctly instead.
